It qualifies only if OFF-SCREEN (true somewhere the player is not looking — probably the main case, since cards describe the whole position but canvases show one place), TIME-CRITICAL, or CROSS-CUTTING. Notably all three MVP candidates (idle building, unsold output, negative cashflow) FAIL this test now that BL-248 cards show them — evidence the roster must be rebuilt from play, not inherited from MENU.md. Also settled as a trap rather than a preference: an alert tracks a CONDITION and clears when it clears, so it is not dismissible as a message — you fix it or mute the class, never the instance.
items.design:
DEFERRED ON PURPOSE 2026-08-01 (Ben, during the NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass — see NR-012).

## Where this came from

MENU.md's Slot 1 MVP originally named ALERTS as one of four roll-ups — idle buildings, unsold output, negative cashflow — and noted in passing that it introduces an "alert" concept the game does not otherwise have.

Ben's 2026-07-31 call replaced that MVP four with the exemplar's Production / Trade / Workforce / Finance. The promoting session did NOT reintroduce alerts anywhere, so the concept was retired by omission: an idle building and a negative net now read as red verdicts on their own cards instead.

Ben, asked about it directly (2026-08-01): "We can make alerts. I'm not sure where to put them yet, I think we should just defer this item. There's not much info on how the game plays yet, and I'm saving that eval until after we get basic AI which can play the game."

## Why it is parked rather than designed

The open question is not WHETHER alerts exist but WHERE they live and WHAT earns one, and neither can be answered from the current build. Ben's reason is a real methodological one and worth preserving: the game has no opponent, so nobody knows yet which conditions actually surprise a player mid-campaign. An alert roster designed against a world where nothing competes with you would enumerate the wrong things.

So this unparks after the v0.2.0 AI opponent can play the game, when there is play data to read. Do not promote it earlier on the grounds that it is cheap — cheapness is not the constraint here, evidence is.

## What is settled

- Alerts ARE wanted. This is a deferral, not a rejection.
- The current red-verdict treatment stands in the meantime, and is not a placeholder to be apologised for: a red Finance card IS the signal, it simply cannot be enumerated.

## What is open

- **Where they live.** A dedicated dashboard card, a header strip, the comms dock, or a surface that does not exist yet. MENU.md's original placement was a Slot 1 card; that placement is no longer assumed.
- **What earns one.** The MVP named three (idle building, unsold output, negative cashflow). Whether those are the right three is exactly what the post-AI evaluation decides.
- **Whether an alert is dismissible, and whether it persists across ticks.** Untouched.
- **The relationship to red verdicts.** If a card already shows red, an alert repeating it is noise. The alert concept probably has to earn its place by covering what NO card shows — which is an argument for defining it against play, not against the current surfaces.

## Not in scope

Changing the four roll-up cards, which landed with BL-248 and are Ben's chosen set.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the deferral is honoured; what is settled is the CRITERION the later evaluation applies

Ben's reason for parking this is methodological and correct: nobody knows which conditions
surprise a player until something competes with them. That stands, and this item does **not**
unpark.

What can be settled without play data is the **test** the post-AI evaluation will apply — which
turns the wait into a prepared question rather than an open one.

### The criterion: an alert must cover what NO card shows

The item half-states this ("probably has to earn its place by covering what no card shows");
making it the rule.

**If a condition is already visible as a red verdict on a roll-up card, it does not earn an
alert.** Repeating it is noise, and noise is how alert systems become ignored — at which point
they are worse than absent, because the player has learned to dismiss the channel that was
supposed to carry the urgent thing.

An alert earns its place only if the condition is at least one of:

1. **Off-screen** — true on a body or a surface the player is not currently looking at. This is
   the strongest case and probably the main one, since the roll-up cards describe the player's
   whole position but the canvases show one place at a time.
2. **Time-critical** — acting late is materially worse than acting now. A slowly worsening
   margin is a card; a convoy about to arrive at a market that has gone dormant is an alert.
3. **Cross-cutting** — no single card owns it, because it is a relationship between things
   (a supply chain broken across two bodies).

Notably, all three of the MVP's original candidates — idle building, unsold output, negative
cashflow — **fail this test as stated**, because BL-248's cards now show exactly those. That is
not an argument that alerts are unwanted; it is the evidence that the roster has to be
rebuilt from play rather than inherited from MENU.md.

### One more thing settled, because it is a trap rather than a preference

**An alert tracks a CONDITION, not a message. It clears when the condition clears.**

So it is not "dismissible" in the message sense. Dismissing an alert for a problem that is still
true is the failure mode every alert system eventually has, and it is designed out here rather
than discovered: there is nothing to dismiss, because the alert *is* the condition being true.

If the player wants to stop seeing one, they fix it or they mute that alert *class* — a
deliberate, remembered choice — never that instance.

### Unchanged

Still parked. Unparks after the v0.2.0 AI opponent can play the game, on Ben's stated reasoning
(evidence, not cheapness). BL-248's four roll-up cards stay untouched.

items.title: A scoring system — how the player knows whether they are ahead, on what axis, and against whom
items.summary: Opened by Ben 2026-08-01 (NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A): 'vital for a sprint, we didn't design it yet.' Nothing today tells the player how they compare to anyone else. Two constraints already bind any answer: CONCEPT.md forbids an end-game score (falling behind is progressive, so the measure must be a STANDING, not a verdict), and DISCOVERY.md makes rival internals private (so a score over every corp's true balance hands the player information the intelligence model withholds). Absorbs the restored all-corporations table (NR-012), which asks the right question with the wrong content. Six open calls enumerated; none guessed. PROPOSED 2026-08-02 (NR-022, for Ben to ratify): one interlocking answer to all six calls — a coarse publicly-published PROFILE of four actor-agnostic axes (reach / production / capital / market share, NO total ever), computed from VISIBLE information (ground truth would make the two fogs decorative), published diegetically by the market so rivals show as BANDS while your own figures stay exact, scoring corporations on axes that survive the BL-094 nation pivot, meaningful only within a campaign (no leaderboard), feeding credit terms (BL-073) and counterparty routing (BL-037) but deliberately NOT unified with BL-202 AI utility (Goodhart).
items.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass). NOTHING BELOW IS SETTLED. This item states the question, the constraints the existing corpus already imposes on any answer, and the calls Ben has to make. It deliberately does not propose a formula.

## Why it exists

Ben, 2026-08-01: "Open a new item on a scoring system. This is vital for a sprint, we didn't design it yet." Raised while resolving NR-012 — he first said to merge the restored all-corporations balance table INTO the scoring item, then found no such item existed. So the table is this item's first known surface, not a separate concern.

## The actual question

How does a player know whether they are winning?

Today the honest answer is: they cannot. The player can read their own balance, their own buildings and their own runway. Nothing tells them how that compares to anyone else, or whether a rising balance is a good balance for this point in a campaign. The one surface that ever compared corporations was a two-column balance table, and BL-248 deleted it as a duplicate.

## The constraint that shapes every answer: there is no end-game screen

CONCEPT.md is explicit — "There is no end-game screen. You don't 'lose' an Era; you enter the next one underprepared, and it is hard... falling behind is progressive, not a single failure state."

So this is NOT a victory score. A single scalar that resolves at the end of a campaign is the wrong shape for a game whose stated failure mode is gradual. What the game needs is a STANDING measure — am I ahead or behind, on what axis, right now, and is the gap opening or closing.

That reframing matters more than the formula. A score you can only read at the end teaches nothing; a standing that moves each tick is a feedback signal the player can act on, which is what "stagnation as loss" requires to be legible at all.

## The constraint that limits what can be scored: rival internals are PRIVATE

DISCOVERY.md § competitor visibility (BL-068) settles that rival buildings are visible, rival internals are private, and markets are public. The activity fog (BL-089) further gates what the player knows about a body at all.

This is the sharpest constraint on the item, and the one most likely to be violated by accident: a score computed from every corporation's true balance is information the player is NOT entitled to. The restored corporations table shows exactly that — every rival's balance, exact, unconditionally. It predates the intelligence model.

So any scoring surface has to answer: is the score computed from what the player can SEE, or from ground truth? A visible-information score is honest and makes intelligence valuable; a ground-truth score is simpler and quietly makes BL-068/BL-089 decorative.

## The constraint on the AI side: a score is an objective function

BL-202 landed a deterministic scored-utility layer for corp AI, and the standing rules bound what background corporations may do. If the player-facing score and the AI's utility score are the SAME quantity, the AI is optimising exactly what the player is measured on — which is either elegant or a Goodhart trap, depending on how coarse the measure is. If they are DIFFERENT quantities, the game measures the player on something no opponent is trying to win. Both readings are defensible; the item must not leave this implicit.

## Open calls — Ben's, all of them

1. **WHO is scored.** Corporations only (the player's peers), nations, or both on separate axes. The prototype's player is a corporation; BL-094 pivots the player to a nation at v0.2.0, so a corporation-only design has a known expiry.
2. **ONE number or a PROFILE.** A single standing is legible and comparable; a profile (reach / production / capital / market share) matches a 4X where players win differently and refuses to imply a single race. The profile reading fits CONCEPT's "corner a market and win early WITHIN an Era" better than a scalar does.
3. **DIEGETIC or META.** Is the score something the world produces — a published ranking, a trade-press table, a credit rating other actors react to — or an out-of-world readout for the player alone? A diegetic score can feed mechanics (credit terms, counterparty preference via BL-037) and is the more characterful option; a meta score cannot be gamed by the fiction and is far cheaper.
4. **VISIBLE-INFORMATION or GROUND-TRUTH inputs.** See the privacy constraint above.
5. **What it FEEDS.** A number nobody reacts to is chrome. Candidates: BL-261 (alerts), the AI's target selection, credit/interest terms (FINANCE.md), nation sentiment (BL-225).
6. **Whether it is comparable ACROSS seeds.** A score that means the same thing on a rich and a poor world requires normalisation against what the world could support; one that does not is only readable within a campaign. This decides whether the number can ever be a leaderboard or is strictly a standing.

## What this item absorbs

**The all-corporations table (NR-012).** Restored 2026-08-01 after BL-248 deleted it, and provisionally parked on nav slot 8 (Diplomacy) with its own flag `show_corporations_table`. It is the rough first draft of this item's surface — the right question (how does each corporation compare) with the wrong content (raw private balances, two columns, no context). Do not treat it as an independent surface to polish: it either becomes this item's comparison view or it is retired BY this item, and either way its home moves off slot 8.

## Determinism

Whatever the formula, it is simulation-visible and must be deterministic: integer/fixed-point accumulation, an explicit tie-break, and no iteration over unordered containers without a sorted walk. The same rule BL-222's first-industrialiser argmax carries.

## Read before promoting

docs/CONCEPT.md § How an Era ends (no end-game screen; stagnation as loss), docs/ui/DISCOVERY.md § competitor visibility, docs/economy/FINANCE.md, src/world/corp_ai.hpp (BL-202's utility layer), and BL-094 (the v0.2.0 nation pivot, which decides whether a corporation-only score has a future).

## PROPOSED 2026-08-02 — one coherent answer to all six calls, for Ben to ratify or overturn

The item says the calls are Ben's, all of them, and that stands — this section does not
overrule it. What it does is refuse to leave six blanks, because the six are **not
independent**: answering call 4 very nearly forces call 3, which shapes call 2, which
dissolves call 1's stated expiry. Six separate questions have a combinatorial answer space;
one interlocking package can actually be judged. Recorded as a decision-taken (NR-022) so it
is overturnable rather than quietly becoming precedent.

The shape, in one sentence: **a coarse, publicly-published PROFILE of four axes, computed from
information the player is entitled to see, feeding credit and counterparty terms, meaningful
only within a campaign.**

### Call 4 first — VISIBLE INFORMATION. This one is nearly forced.

Taking it first because it constrains the rest. The item states the risk exactly: a score over
every corporation's true balance "quietly makes BL-068/BL-089 decorative". That is not a close
trade. Discovery is a designed pillar with its own authority doc, two independent fogs and a
body-level visibility tier; a scoreboard reading ground truth would hand the player, for free
and continuously, the precise thing the entire intelligence model is built to meter.

Ground truth is simpler. It is simpler the way deleting the fog is simpler.

**The objection, answered.** A visible-information score is mostly *unknown* in the early game,
when the player has few routes and little presence. That reads as a defect and is actually the
best property of the design: **not knowing where you stand is itself the signal that you have
not invested in knowing.** It gives intelligence a payoff the player can feel (the standing
sharpens as your commercial sphere grows), and it makes the fog a thing you play against
rather than a thing you wait out. A score fully legible on turn one has nothing left to reveal.

### Call 3 — DIEGETIC, because call 4 demands a source

Once the score is computed from public information, it needs somewhere public to be computed.
"The player privately aggregates what they happen to know" is incoherent as a comparison —
comparisons need a common basis.

**So the world publishes it.** DISCOVERY.md already settles that *markets are public*, which is
exactly the substrate a published ranking may legitimately aggregate: traded volumes, cleared
prices, delivered tonnage, visible holdings. A trade-press table / exchange standing / credit
rating is a diegetic object that can honestly exist in 1960 and can honestly see only what the
market saw.

This also resolves the privacy tension rather than dodging it, by splitting resolution:

- **Your own figures: exact.** You read your balance to the credit.
- **Everyone else's: banded.** A rating, a rank, a coarse tier — never a number.

That is how real ratings work, it is trivially cheaper to compute than an exact rival figure,
and it is honest about what an outside observer could know. It also means the surface can show
every corporation without lying, which the restored table (NR-012) could not.

Ben's standing preference for the deeper option over the cheaper one is a factor here and is
named rather than assumed — meta is genuinely less work, and this recommends against it.

### Call 2 — a PROFILE of four axes, not one number

The item already argues this fits a 4X where players win differently, and CONCEPT's "corner a
market and win early within an Era" is a *narrow* victory a scalar would average away. Two
further reasons:

1. **A scalar implies a race with one finish line, which is precisely the end-game framing
   CONCEPT forbids.** A profile cannot be read as a verdict because there is no single thing to
   be ahead on. The shape of the measure enforces the design constraint by construction,
   instead of relying on nobody adding a total later.
2. **A profile degrades gracefully under partial information.** Under call 4 the player will
   often know a rival's market share and not their capital. A profile shows three axes and a
   gap; a scalar would need to fabricate the missing term or refuse to display.

Proposed axes — deliberately four, deliberately public-observable:

- **Reach** — bodies and markets you are present in.
- **Production** — physical output delivered, by volume.
- **Capital** — banded rating, not a balance.
- **Market share** — share of cleared volume in the goods you trade.

**No aggregate row. No total. Ever.** State it in the item, because a total is the single
change that would convert this back into the victory score CONCEPT rules out, and it is the
change someone will propose as a convenience.

### Call 1 — CORPORATIONS now, and the stated expiry dissolves

The item worries a corporation-only design has a known expiry at BL-094 (the v0.2.0 nation
pivot). It does — but only if the axes are corporation-shaped. All four above are
**actor-agnostic**: a nation has reach, production, capital standing and market share in
exactly the same senses.

**So score CORPORATIONS as the scored actor now, with axes that survive the pivot**, and BL-094
changes who appears in the table, not what the table measures. That is a cheap property to have
and an expensive one to retrofit, which is the whole reason to name it at design time.

Nations are not scored in the prototype — they are the saturated background substrate
(GENERATION_STRATEGY.md's economic premise), not competitors, and ranking them against the
player would misdescribe the game being played.

### Call 6 — WITHIN a campaign only. Not comparable across seeds.

Normalising against what a world *could* support would require a total-potential figure that is
(a) expensive to compute, (b) itself private information under call 4, and (c) meaningless
under CONCEPT's no-end-game framing — there is no context in which two campaigns get compared.

A standing is relative to the rivals on *this* world. That is what "am I ahead, and is the gap
opening" needs and it needs nothing more. **This forecloses a leaderboard**, which nothing has
asked for and which the no-end-game rule would have made incoherent anyway.

### Call 5 — it feeds CREDIT and COUNTERPARTY terms, and is NOT the AI's utility function

A number nobody reacts to is chrome, and the diegetic choice earns its extra cost only if the
world acts on it. Two hooks already exist and need no new system:

- **Credit terms.** FINANCE.md's debt interest (BL-073) currently has no risk input. A capital
  standing is exactly a risk input, and "your rating slipped so your borrowing got dearer" is a
  consequence the player can feel and act on.
- **Counterparty preference.** BL-037's preferred-seller routing already picks between sellers.
  Standing is a legitimate tiebreak, and it makes reputation mechanical.

**Kept separate from BL-202's AI utility, deliberately** — the item asks that this not be left
implicit. They are different quantities and must stay so:

- BL-202's utility is an **internal optimiser over ground truth**; the corp AI knows its own
  books exactly.
- The standing is a **coarse public view** built from what the market saw.

If they were unified, every AI would be directly optimising the published number, which is the
Goodhart trap the item names — and worse, it would require the AI to read a public aggregate it
has no reason to care about. Different quantities is both the safer answer and the more truthful
one. The AI may *read* standing as one input to target selection (who is worth competing
against), which is the honest use of a public figure.

### What this does to NR-012's restored table

It is retired **as it stands** and replaced by this item's profile view — the right question, now
with content it is entitled to show. Concretely: rival rows lose their exact balances and gain
four banded axes; the player's own row keeps exact figures. Its home moves off nav slot 8
(Diplomacy), as the item already requires.

### Determinism

Unchanged and load-bearing. Banding is a deterministic bucketing of a fixed-point quantity with
explicit boundaries (a value exactly on a boundary must land in a defined band — do not leave it
to float comparison), ranks have an explicit tie-break, and any walk over corporations is a
sorted walk. Same rule as BL-222's first-industrialiser argmax.

### Still genuinely open after this

- **The band boundaries and axis normalisation** — real tuning, wants the live economy, not a
  paragraph. Promote with placeholder bands and tune against a running campaign.
- **Where the profile lives on screen.** BL-266 has just settled that the Selection band rests on
  the player's own corporation, which is the natural host for the player's OWN standing; the
  comparison view across all corporations is a ledger. That split looks right but is a layout
  call and is Ben's.

## RATIFIED 2026-08-03 (Ben, NR-022)

Ben ratified the six-call package **as written** — no substitutions. The diegetic publication
route is confirmed (not the cheaper meta route), the four-axis profile stands with **no total
ever**, and rival figures stay **banded** rather than exact. The banding is the load-bearing
piece: it is what lets a comparison surface show every corporation at once without violating
BL-068's competitor-visibility rule, which the restored NR-012 table could not do.

The item is promote-ready as designed; nothing further is owed from Ben on it.
items.resolution: FIRST SLICE LANDED 2026-08-06 (docs/development/req/requirements.json § corp-standing-profile): src/world/standing.{hpp,cpp} computes reach/capital/market-share, banded for rivals (never a number), exact for the player, no total row ever — src/ui/corporation_panel.cpp's old raw-balance table retired. standing_harness 41/41 PASS. Kept a SEPARATE quantity from corp_ai's utility scorer per Call 5. Status stays 'designed', not 'complete': the production axis (BL-262's fourth) is deferred — no honest visible-information source exists in the engine today (rival recipe/workforce are private under BL-068) — and the credit-terms/counterparty hooks (Call 5's 'what it feeds') are unbuilt. A follow-on item should be filed for those once a visible production proxy is designed.

items.title: Markets emerge at runtime when colonisation or exploration reaches a body, instead of being fixed at world-gen
items.summary: Ben's answer to NR-004 (2026-08-01): 'markets should be spontaneously generated when colonisation / exploration starts.' Today every market seeds on the home body at world-gen and nothing creates one at runtime, so the generated world can never record an inter-body trade route — the blind spot BL-254 worked around with stub markets, and the reason BL-248's Trade card reads 0 lanes forever. Makes markets simulation state rather than a generation artifact, which reaches the save format, determinism, catchment routing and price discovery with no history. Five open calls, chief among them the mechanical trigger and what actually clears at an outpost market with supply and no local demand. SETTLED 2026-08-02 (all five calls): TRIGGER is the first BUILDING placed on a body — investment not presence, because a visit produces nothing to clear and placement is already a clean deterministic event (survey completion is explicitly NOT the trigger; that is the geographic fog, and the two axes stay independent). ANY corporation can cause one, and a rival-created market on an unvisited body enters at the fog Unknown tier — the player does not learn of it for free, which gives BL-089 its first consequential secret. ONE market per body off-world (BL-096 carving is population-anchored and an outpost has none). Markets NEVER disappear — they go dormant, which the Stale tier already models and which avoids id-reuse aliasing across saves. Outpost markets clear against INTER-BODY demand, not local population, with opening prices seeded from BL-191 haul-distance pricing then handed to EMA once history exists — which is the answer to the "prices collapse to the floor" failure the item flagged.
items.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass, resolving NR-004).

## The finding that raised it

Every market seeds on the single tiled body (Kepler). MARKETS.md states it plainly: "Markets exist only on the home body (Kepler) today; Cinder, Selene, and Pallas carry none" and "Markets are fixed at world-gen — nothing creates or destroys one at runtime."

A `trade_route` is body-level, so an intra-body lane records nothing. Together those two facts mean the generated world CANNOT record a trade route however long it runs, independent of the launchpad gate. BL-254's data-creep harness had to author three stub markets before its run to give its convoy lanes endpoints at all — an instrument working around the world rather than measuring it, which is the signal that raised NR-004.

The player-visible half is NR-013: the BL-248 Trade roll-up correctly reads "0 lanes" on a fresh campaign, and would keep reading it forever.

## Ben's answer

"I think markets should be spontaneously generated when colonisation / exploration starts." (2026-08-01)

So none of NR-004's three options was taken. The premise is not "Era 0 has no off-world markets, document it" and not "pre-seed a market elsewhere" — it is that market EXISTENCE becomes a runtime consequence of the player (or a rival) going somewhere. A market is not scenery placed at world-gen; it is what appears once there is something to trade at a place.

That is a better answer than either option offered, and it is worth saying why: pre-seeding a market on an empty moon would have created a destination with no cause, which is the same lying-figure objection Ben raised against showing invented continents in the wizard preview (BL-256). Spontaneous generation keeps the world honest — a market exists exactly when the fiction says one would.

## What this changes structurally

Markets stop being a world-gen artifact and become simulation state. That is the load-bearing consequence and it touches:

- **Serialisation.** The save format must carry markets that did not exist at generation. Flat binary, per TECH_FOUNDATIONS — a count-prefixed run, not an assumption that market ids match generation order.
- **Determinism.** Creation must be a deterministic function of world state, not of iteration order. Sorted walks over any unordered container; an explicit tie-break if two candidate sites qualify on the same tick.
- **`market_for_tile` / `market_for_corp_on_body` catchment.** Both resolve against a fixed set today. A market appearing mid-campaign re-points catchment for tiles that previously had none — or, on the home body, potentially re-points tiles away from an existing centre. Decide whether new markets can ever steal catchment or only claim unserved ground.
- **Price discovery with no history.** `resolve_price` uses a price band and EMA smoothing over past prices. A market created on tick 400 has no past. Its opening prices have to come from somewhere — `base_price`, the nearest market, or the haul-distance pricing BL-191 already does for endemic goods.

## Open calls — Ben's

1. **The TRIGGER.** "When colonisation / exploration starts" needs a mechanical reading. Candidates: the first building placed on a body; a population presence; a completed convoy arrival; a survey (BL-067) completing. The choice decides whether a market is a consequence of INVESTMENT (a building) or of PRESENCE (a visit), and those give very different games.
2. **WHO can cause one.** Player only, any corporation, or a nation. If rivals can, the activity fog (BL-089) has to say whether the player learns of a market they did not create — a market appearing on a body the player has never visited is either intelligence they should not have, or a good reason to go and look.
3. **ONE market per body, or the resource-carved multi-market model (BL-096) applied off-world?** The carved model is population-anchored, and an off-world outpost has effectively none. One market per body is the simple reading and probably right until population exists off-world.
4. **Does a market ever DISAPPEAR?** If the last building on a body is decommissioned, does its market persist with stale prices, or vanish? Persisting is kinder to the activity fog's Stale tier (DISCOVERY.md) and avoids a save-format edge; vanishing is truer.
5. **What CLEARS there.** The clearing model is fed by production and population demand. An outpost market has supply and nearly no local demand, so without inter-body flow its prices collapse to the floor immediately. This is the question most likely to make the feature read as broken on first play, and it should be answered before implementation rather than discovered.

## Consequences for existing items

- **BL-254 (data-creep convoy scenario)** — its harness pre-authors three stub markets to work around exactly this. Once markets can emerge, decide whether the harness drives the real trigger instead of stubbing, which would make it a genuine end-to-end check rather than a synthetic one.
- **NR-013 / BL-248** — the Trade roll-up stops being permanently zero, which removes the "dashboard quarter that always says nothing" problem without a UI change.
- **BL-088 (persistent trade routes) / BL-089 (activity fog)** — both describe machinery that currently has nothing to act on. This is the item that gives them a first cause.
- **ERAS.md** — Era 0 being terrestrial is unchanged; this item does not open space access, it says what happens to markets once access exists.

## Read before promoting

docs/economy/MARKETS.md (§ Market centres and seeding, § The clearing tick), docs/ui/DISCOVERY.md (activity fog + competitor visibility), docs/economy/ERAS.md, src/world/hard_coded_world.cpp (the BL-096 seeding pass), and BL-254.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the five open calls, answered as one model

### 1. TRIGGER — the first BUILDING placed on a body. Investment, not presence.

The item frames the choice exactly: investment or presence, "and those give very different
games". Investment wins on three counts.

**A market needs something to trade.** A visit produces nothing to clear, so a
presence-triggered market opens empty and stays empty until someone builds anyway — the
trigger fires early and the feature does not start working until the building lands regardless.
Investment makes the trigger and the first useful moment the same moment.

**Placement is already a clean mechanical event.** It is validated, deterministic, and
single-tick — `market appears on the tick the first building completes` needs no new concept.
"Exploration starts" would need defining (a convoy arriving? a survey completing? a unit
entering?), and each candidate is a different fuzzy edge.

**It is the better game.** A market that appears because someone committed capital is a
consequence the player caused; one that appears because someone looked is scenery with a
delayed spawn. Ben's own objection to pre-seeding — a destination with no cause — applies
almost as strongly to presence.

Survey completion (BL-067) is explicitly **not** the trigger. Surveying is the geographic fog;
market existence is commercial. Keeping them separate preserves DISCOVERY.md's two-independent-
axes rule.

### 2. WHO — any corporation. And the player does NOT automatically learn of it.

Restricting creation to the player would make rivals scenery, which contradicts the whole
premise of competing corporations.

The activity fog answers the intelligence half, and this is where the item's worry resolves
into a feature: **a market created by a rival on a body the player has never visited enters at
the fog's Unknown tier.** The player does not learn of it for free. They learn by going, by a
trade route reaching it, or not at all.

That is the same argument BL-262 (scoring) settles on: information the player is entitled to
is what the surfaces show, and anything else makes BL-089 decorative. It also gives the fog its
first genuinely consequential secret — a rival market you have not found is a real
disadvantage, not a greyed tile.

### 3. ONE market per body off-world

BL-096's resource-carved multi-market model is **population-anchored**, and an off-world outpost
has effectively no population to anchor to. Carving with no population is carving on an
arbitrary axis.

One market per body off-world; the home body keeps its carved multi-market seeding unchanged.
Revisit if and when off-world population exists — at which point the carved model applies for
the reason it was designed, rather than by analogy.

### 4. DISAPPEAR — no. It persists and goes dormant.

Three reasons, in increasing order of weight:

1. **The fog already has the concept.** DISCOVERY.md's **Stale** tier is exactly "this existed,
   my information is old". A dormant market is what Stale is for.
2. **It avoids a save-format edge.** Deleting markets means either id reuse (which will
   eventually alias two different markets across a save/load) or tombstones (which is
   persistence with extra steps). Count-prefixed runs of live markets is simpler than either.
3. **It is truer, not less true.** The item calls vanishing "truer"; it is not. An abandoned
   exchange does not become a place that never traded. Prices go stale, nobody clears, the
   record remains — which is what actually happens to a market town when the mine closes.

Surface it as **dormant**, not as an active market with frozen prices — a market showing last
quarter's prices as if current is a lying figure.

### 5. WHAT CLEARS — remote demand, and haul-distance opening prices

This is the call the item flags as most likely to make the feature read as broken, and it is
right: an outpost has supply and almost no local demand, so a market clearing only against
local population collapses to the floor on tick one.

**An outpost market clears primarily against INTER-BODY demand** — the pull of the home body's
markets through convoy routes — not against local population. That is not a special case bolted
on; it is what an outpost market *is*. Nobody builds a mine on a moon to sell to the moon.

**Opening prices come from BL-191's haul-distance pricing, not from `base_price` and not from
EMA.** The machinery already exists for endemic goods, and it is the right source for the same
reason: a price at a distant body should reflect what it costs to get the good to where demand
is. `base_price` would open every outpost at the same price regardless of distance;
EMA cannot run with no history.

So the price-discovery hole the item names has an answer that adds no new mechanism: **seed from
haul-distance, then let EMA take over once there is history to smooth.**

### Consequences, confirmed

- **BL-254's harness should drive the real trigger** once this lands — place a building, get a
  market — which converts it from a synthetic check into a genuine end-to-end one. That is the
  whole reason NR-004 was raised.
- **NR-013 / BL-248's Trade roll-up** stops being permanently zero with no UI change.
- **BL-088 / BL-089** get their first cause, as the item says.
- **ERAS.md** unchanged — this says what happens to markets once access exists, not when access
  arrives.

### Determinism

Creation is a function of world state, evaluated at one fixed point in the tick, with a sorted
walk over bodies and an explicit tie-break if two qualify simultaneously. Market ids must be
allocated from a monotonic counter carried in the save, **not** from container size — the latter
aliases after any removal and is the exact bug the persist-don't-delete rule above already
avoids.
items.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. All five of Ben's settled calls implemented as specified: TRIGGER is the first building COMPLETING on a body with no market (maybe_spawn_market, called from both construct_building's instant-completion path and run_construction's pacing-loop completion, not placement) — survey completion is explicitly not the trigger, keeping the geographic/commercial fogs independent. ANY corporation can cause one (no player-only gate); a rival-created market on an unvisited body relies on the existing activity fog (BL-089) for its Unknown-tier gating — no new fog code needed, since fog visibility already reads presence/routes, not market existence directly. ONE market per body off-world (checked via a market_for_body scan before spawning); the home body's BL-096 carved seeding is untouched. Markets NEVER disappear — no deletion code exists or was added; dormancy falls out of the ordinary zero-supply/zero-demand clearing case. Opening prices seeded from the home market's own base_price marked up by a distance proxy (|orbital_radius_au difference|, moon-approximated at its parent — NOT the precise tick-pure angular distance supply_system.cpp's convoy routing uses, which only matters for real haul cost/speed, not a price curve). WHAT CLEARS: new inject_interbody_demand pulls a distance-discounted slice of the home body's own unmet demand onto every outpost market each tick (economy.market_emergence in Lua), preventing the price-floor collapse the design flagged as the likeliest failure mode; existing dispatch_convoys physical routing is untouched and independent. New market_emergence_harness (16/16 PASS): no market before any building, spawn on completion, correct centre_tile, exact opening-price and pulled-demand formulas, no second market on a second building, no self-pull on the home market, and a graceful all-zero-price degenerate fixture with no home market (no crash). Full ProjectIo build clean; econ_harness/econ_stability/resource_chain_harness/determinism_harness/construction_harness/world_audit/construction_gate_harness/buildings_rework_harness/multi_building_tile_harness/population_demand_harness/habitability_tranche_harness/supply_advance/trade_routes_harness/commercial_fog_harness all rerun clean. ai_skill_harness rebuilt fresh and rerun: identical 8 failures to the BL-366-only baseline, confirming BL-263 (and BL-368) do not move those bands further — corrected an earlier stale-exe misreading, see NR-169. No save-format work: no general serialisation system exists yet in this codebase to extend (no src/world/serialisation.cpp), so that half of the design is deferred until the general save seam lands, not part of this item's scope. docs/economy/MARKETS.md gains § Spontaneous market emergence.

items.title: The New World wizard's layout after per-stage folding — fill the reserved band, size and centre the folded stages, buttons over dropdowns, Esc to close
items.summary: Low priority, filed at Ben's explicit request (NR-015, 2026-08-02): 'it works fine now - just visually awkward.' Per-stage folding left the wizard's chart region sized for charts it no longer draws at rest, so four verdict lines sit above a large empty band on the first screen a new player sees. Ben's direction: the BL-256 globe fills the space, folded stages get bigger and are vertically centred as a group, preference controls become buttons rather than dropdowns, and Esc closes an expanded view. That last one is genuinely missing — handle_key returns early unless the screen is in_game, so the whole Esc ladder is unreachable in the wizard. Hold behind BL-256; sizes must be reported to Ben as measurements before anyone picks one. SETTLED 2026-08-02: on the generation screen Esc folds an expanded stage and does NOTHING else — round-stepping belongs to a visible Back control, not a hidden key that discards choices, and leaving the wizard is destructive and would need its own confirm rung. With nothing expanded Esc is deliberately inert. Implementation constraint: do NOT lift handle_key early return (it is what stops Space/1-5/canvas commands firing against a null world) — add a ten-line generation-screen key path instead. The Rule 0b measurement gate stands and discharges at promotion, not now, since BL-256 will have changed the layout being measured. Now requires BL-256.
items.design:
LOW PRIORITY, DEFERRED ON PURPOSE — opened 2026-08-02 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-015). Ben: "I'm considering changing this later, so just mark it as a low priority item in the backlog, since it works fine now - just visually awkward." Nothing here is urgent and nothing is broken. Do not promote this ahead of work that fixes something.

## The symptom

BL-214's per-stage folding landed on the New World wizard and made the generation chain legible at a glance for the first time — a round's four stages read as four verdict lines. But the chart region is still SIZED for full charts, so at rest those four lines sit at the top of a tall band that is otherwise empty, above the preference block (capture: fold_wizard_stages_folded).

The layout reserves height for charts that are no longer drawn at rest. It works; it looks under-filled. This is the first surface a new player sees, which is the only reason it is filed at all.

## Ben's four directions

Given as the shape of a later fix, not as a specification:

1. **The pre-gen "map" fills the space.** BL-256 (generation globe) is the substantive answer — the globe becomes the generation screen's primary view and occupies the band, with the folded stages reading as extras on top of it. This item should NOT invent a different filler; if BL-256 lands first, most of the awkwardness goes with it.
2. **Each expandable item gets bigger**, so a folded stage is a substantial thing rather than a thin line.
3. **The group is vertically centred**, so the folded set sits in the middle of its band instead of clinging to the top edge with dead space beneath.
4. **Buttons rather than dropdowns.** The wizard's preference controls become direct choices instead of combos — one click instead of open-then-pick, and every option visible without a menu.

## Esc on the generation screen — genuinely missing today

Ben also asked for Esc to close these views. That is NOT already covered by BL-214's Esc rung, and the reason is worth recording because it is easy to assume otherwise: `app::handle_key` returns early when `m_screen != app_screen::in_game` ("No game bindings on the menu or the generation screen"), so the entire Esc ladder — including the fold rung added for BL-214 — is unreachable while the wizard is up. A stage expanded in the wizard can only be closed by its chevron.

So this needs a deliberate decision about what Esc means BEFORE a game exists, not just an extra rung. Candidates, in order: fold an expanded stage; step back a wizard round; leave the wizard for the main menu. The first is clearly wanted; the other two are a navigation model the wizard does not currently have, and adopting them by accident would be worse than leaving Esc inert.

## Measurements owed before anyone builds this (Rule 0b)

"Bigger" and "vertically centred" are exactly the ambiguous-measurement case the standing rules name. Before implementing, report to Ben the CURRENT numbers with units — the chart region's reserved height, a folded stage row's height, the gap left empty at rest, and the preference block's height — and let him state the target against real figures rather than prose. Do not pick a multiplier.

## Sequencing

Hold this behind BL-256 (generation globe). Direction 1 is the real fix and the other three are adjustments to a layout the globe would restructure anyway; doing them first means doing them twice. If BL-256 stalls, directions 2-4 plus the Esc rung stand on their own as a smaller pass.

## Not in scope

The content of the charts, the fold idiom itself (BL-214, settled), and the wizard's round structure. This is a layout and input item only.

## Chevron alignment (Ben, 2026-08-02)

"Chevrons should be left aligned. It doesn't make sense to have the user move the mouse that far for a similar action."

The cost being named is travel: a control that sits at the far right of a wide band makes the player cross the whole width to do the same thing they just did on the row above. On the wizard that band is the full chart region, so the trip is at its worst there.

RESOLVED 2026-08-02, and it was not the conflict it first looked like. Ben clarified that the left-aligned control he meant is the RETURN control of a full-canvas view (`‹ title`, top left), not a row's expander. A foldable ROW puts its controls in a right-hand gutter: `Expandable item … ⌄ ›`, aligned to a fixed column so a long title never moves them. BL-265 carries the settled vocabulary; this item follows it rather than restating it. The travel-cost point still stands and is what the gutter answers — the controls are in ONE predictable column, so the hand learns one destination instead of hunting per surface.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — what Esc means before a game exists

Chevron alignment was already resolved and sequencing already stated. One thing was open, and
the item was right that it is a decision rather than an extra rung.

### Esc folds an expanded stage. That is ALL it does on the generation screen.

Of the three candidates the item lists, only the first is adopted:

- **Fold an expanded stage** — yes. Clearly wanted, and it restores the symmetry the rest of
  the app has (BL-265's takeover rung does exactly this in game).
- **Step back a wizard round** — no. The wizard has no back-navigation model, and Esc is the
  wrong place to invent one. If round-stepping is wanted it is an explicit **Back** control,
  visible, next to the forward control — not a hidden key that silently discards a round's
  choices.
- **Leave the wizard for the main menu** — no, and least of all silently. Abandoning a
  part-configured world is a destructive action on a keypress with no confirmation. If it is
  wanted later it needs the same exit-confirm rung the in-game ladder already has.

**With nothing expanded, Esc is inert.** Deliberately: an inert key is honest, and each rejected
candidate is a navigation model the wizard would then owe in full.

### The implementation constraint — do NOT lift the early return

`app::handle_key` returns early when `m_screen != app_screen::in_game`, which is why the whole
Esc ladder is unreachable in the wizard. The tempting one-line fix is to lift or loosen that
guard.

**Don't.** That guard is what stops in-game bindings firing on a screen with no world — Space
pausing a simulation that is not running, 1-5 setting a speed, the canvas-command path
dispatching against a null world. Loosening it to get one rung exposes all of them.

**Add a small generation-screen key path instead**, handling exactly one key and one action:
Esc, when a stage is expanded, folds it. Ten lines that cannot leak, rather than a guard change
that can.

### The measurement gate stands

The item's Rule 0b note is not discharged by this settlement and is not meant to be: "bigger"
and "vertically centred" still need current numbers reported to Ben before anyone picks a
value. That happens at **promotion**, against the layout as it stands then — which, if BL-256
lands first, will not be the layout measured today. Measuring now would be measuring something
about to be replaced.

`requires` updated to include BL-256, matching the sequencing the item already states in prose.

items.title: Expand and full screen become two controls, full screen takes the canvas rather than the window, and a full-screened accordion scrolls all its items
items.summary: SETTLED 2026-08-02. Ben’s revision of BL-214's binary fold model after using it (NR-016, 2026-08-02). Four changes: (1) one chevron becomes two controls — expand shows a graph or an accordion of graphs IN PLACE, full screen is the takeover; (2) full screen is bounded to the CANVAS region rather than the whole window, so the shell chrome, clock and selection survive and a ledger going full screen becomes the same kind of event as descending the zoom ladder; (3) a full-screened accordion must scroll ALL its items open, since 'anything full screen deserves its full space'; (4) the controls must occupy one predictable column — today two call sites draw the chevron left of the label and two push it to the right edge. Change 4 is settled: a row shows `title … ⌄ ›` with both controls right-aligned to a fixed gutter so they line up across rows, and the full-canvas view shows `‹ title` with a single return control top-left. The rule to carry into LAYOUT.md — controls that operate on an item in a list are right-gutter-aligned; the control that leaves a view is top-left. SETTLED 2026-08-02: the state model splits (takeover stays single-target, in-place becomes a set), the takeover ignores in-place state and restores it on return, Esc gains only the takeover rung, ledger-plus-takeover coexistence is intended, ui::canvas_rect() is added as task 1 (three ad-hoc derivations exist today and no canvas rect does), and both new controls draw their glyphs rather than typing them (BL-234).

items.title: The Selection element is always open — retire dismissal, drop the Esc hide rung, and design the empty state
items.summary: Ben's call (NR-017, 2026-08-02): the Selection element should never be hidden, so Esc's terminal rung becomes the pause screen rather than a dismissal. Dismissal was right for BL-194/195/196's floating card over an open canvas with the minimap as anchor; BL-213's fixed bottom band plus a shell that now fills the perimeter turns the same affordance into a hole in the frame. Removes the Esc hide rung and selection_hidden_for, and — the real work — decides the empty state, which has never been designed because nothing draws today when nothing is selected. BL-194/195/196 annotated stale on their dismissal half, not rewritten. SETTLED 2026-08-02: the band rests on the PLAYER’S OWN CORPORATION (builder already exists at selection_panel.cpp — no invented content; keeps deselect representable, which the always-selected option could not; natural future host for BL-262 scoring). The pause screen IS show_system_menu, not a new surface — nothing to build for Esc to land sensibly. Difficulty raised 2->3: selection_hidden_for has eleven call sites, not one.

items.title: GPU utilisation + multicore CPU threading — the growing generation/rendering cost needs to stop landing on one core
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-02, immediately after seeing the BL-170 river render live: "All these items are starting to cause CPU lag though." Filed SSS (do-immediately) per his instruction. Everything the engine does today — sim tick, world generation, and now the canvas draw loop (roads, borders, rivers, markers, all per-tile per-frame) — runs on one core with no GPU compute path, and each session keeps adding another always-on per-tile pass to that same single thread. This item is the ask to stop that trend; it does not yet say how, since GPU-vs-CPU-parallel is a real architectural fork that deserves its own design pass rather than a guessed answer landed under lag pressure.

items.title: Planetary canvas pays O(all 15,120 tiles) per frame — reuse the cached raster index and cull per-tile work to the visible rows
items.summary: The executable half of BL-267's measurement verdict (2026-08-02): the planetary draw loop rebuilds a 15,120-entry hash index of the active body's tiles every frame, re-sorts a 15k id list every frame, and runs full lens/colour work on every tile before any visibility test — flat ~11 ms (Release) / ~40 ms (Debug) regardless of zoom. Fix: read the raster index logistics already caches on world (body_tile_grid), iterate it row-major (identical draw order — tile ids ascend row-major from generation), cull to the visible row range, and hoist the existing horizontal wrap-window test above the per-tile lens work. Pixel-identical by construction; verified by the existing goldens plus a pan_perf A/B.

items.title: Whole-grid view is vertex-emission-bound (~155k verts of hexes) — LOD or cached terrain layer for the zoomed-out planetary canvas
items.summary: The residual BL-268 (canvas cull + cache) deliberately did not chase: with the whole 180x84 grid visible, all 15,120 hexes are genuinely on-screen and ImGui emits ~155k vertices every frame — 12.1 ms work/frame in Release (over the 8 ms audit target; fine against 16.7). Per-tile culling cannot help when everything is visible; the fix is emitting less: coarser geometry at low zoom (hexes to quads/points below a zoom threshold) or caching the static terrain layer to a texture redrawn only on lens/fog/built change. Filed per planetary-pan-perf R4 rather than stretching BL-268. Priority B: the case is the min-zoom overview, where 12 ms still holds 60 fps; it misses only the stricter 8 ms average target.

items.title: The action dictionary — every control in the game: typed arguments, preconditions, expected output, and reason to select, so an AI plays via words
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-02, filed SSS per his instruction ('it blocks the next most important milestone, which is a word-based procedural generation and later gameplay'): a complete dictionary giving every button press A) expected output and B) reason to select, so an LLM plays via words — the model that will eventually run on-machine, and first a cloud Sonnet/Opus experiment. Scope settled by elicitation same day: EVERY control including chrome; entries carry typed arguments + preconditions beyond the A/B pair; store lives in docs/ai/ (the consumer is the AI player); the consumer sequence is BOTH — dictionary now, word-driven generation then word-driven gameplay consume it in order. This is the third catalogue axis: user_stories.json = intent, UX_QUESTIONS (BL-260) = information surfaces, ACTIONS = the action axis. The write channel already speaks this shape (corp_command.hpp: 8 verbs, 'exactly the player's action surface', typed rejections); BL-206's blackboard export is the read channel; the dictionary is the missing middle.

items.title: Era -1 sandbox - run the settlement world at tick time from 0 CE to 2000 CE, as the nation-AI / mil-sim proving ground (Sprint 5 theme)
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-02 from the Ben brainstorm ('use Rome as a sandbox'). The settlement pass (BL-218) already simulates settlement -> industrialisation -> war ONCE, at generation time, then freezes the result. This item promotes it to a running simulation: a YEAR-TICK loop over provinces and nations from 0 CE to the campaign epoch, in which wars, collapses and revolutions recur rather than firing once as checkpoints. PURPOSE IS WRITTEN DOWN AND BOUNDED: this is the proving ground for the nation AI (BL-054's parked runtime half, the BL-155/156 diplomacy/war stubs) and the mil-sim (BL-272), and the instrument for tuning the worlds' 'philosophical development' against a seed spread (BL-275) - it lives behind a harness flag / tools target, never in the shipped campaign path, and it dies into (or is absorbed by) the 1960 era when those systems graduate. TRANSFER CONTRACT stated up front: what transfers to the main era is the ARCHITECTURE (decision loop, spatial reasoning, war/peace evaluation, the combat engine itself), never the tuning constants. Rome is the CALIBRATION REFERENCE, not the content - sea:river:land cost ratios, campaign-season structure (mare-clausum-style closure), army supply radii, plausible hegemony formation speed - while the world itself stays Kepler's own generated antiquity, seed-varied so the AI cannot overfit one map. This item also partially absorbs BL-223's design question: simulating a thousand near-ruptures is how the averted one gets designed against evidence rather than lore.

items.title: Typed units + doctrine-parameter combat - one engine for simulated history AND the main era (overturns the abstract-war decision)
items.summary: OVERTURNED DECISION, recorded here at Ben's instruction rather than parked in NEEDS_REVIEW (Ben, 2026-08-02): since BL-221 the rule has been that simulated-history wars resolve as ABSTRACT scalar comparisons (record_tribal_conflict, the rupture war branch - zeal/dominion/terrain numbers, no units). Ben overturns the abstract half: simulated history uses REAL ancient units and real military tactics, as typed unit types that later exist in the main era. The 'drives, does not narrate' half SURVIVES untouched - battles still move borders, abundance and the record. The strongest argument for the overturn: unit_component in the 1960 game is a stub (count=50, nothing else), so the sandbox does not borrow the main era's military model - it DEFINES it. One combat engine, era-keyed rosters (BL-274), and the 1960 game inherits a mil-sim with two thousand years of regression tests behind it.

items.title: Province demography - population growth, war/plague drawdown, and manpower as the army budget (POPULATION.md's first honest consumer)
items.summary: Armies are population, and the Era -1 sim (BL-271) is unanchored without a manpower model: population centres currently carry a static scale and no growth, so 2000 years of army sizes would float free of anything. This item gives each PROVINCE (the BL-218 unit) a population that grows and is drawn down - the deferred POPULATION.md design finding its first honest consumer, at the coarse granularity the year-tick needs rather than the full agglomeration model the 1960 game eventually wants.

items.title: Era-keyed unit rosters - material-gated unit types (bronze -> iron -> gunpowder -> industrial), unlocked by endowment and industrialisation timing, NOT a tech tree
items.summary: The unit roster must turn over across 2000 years (legion -> cataphract -> pike-and-shot -> rifles) and what unlocks it is MATERIAL - bronze, iron, horses, gunpowder, then coal/steel. Ben's position stands that a player-facing tech tree only works in a 1900s+ start, and this item deliberately is NOT one: it is an AUTHORED ERA TABLE keyed to quantities the settlement pass already computes (ore endowment, industrialisation timing) - the same 'endowment, not virtue' derivation extended to the military layer. The forge-god culture fields iron units early; the first industrialiser fields rifles while its neighbour still fields pike - which is the philosophical-development instrument in one sentence, and the mechanism by which a late-industrialising world FEELS late.
items.design:
## Settled at filing (2026-08-02 brainstorm)

- **An authored table, not a tree**: rows are (era band, unit type, doctrine options, material requirement); a nation's available rows are a pure function of its provinces' endowment classes and its industrialisation year (both already in settlement_state). No research, no player choice, no unlock events - availability is DERIVED, so the roster is explainable from the map the same way ideology is.
- **Material requirements read the existing resource axes**: iron units want ore_q provinces; gunpowder reads the energy class as a proxy until a dedicated saltpetre/sulphur signal exists (a NAMED substitution, per the BL-221 convention of naming stand-ins rather than faking inputs); industrial units want the Stage 4 furnace date.
- **Asymmetry is the point**: two nations at the same date field different rosters because their ground differs - horse-country fields cavalry doctrine, coastal ports field marines and fleets. The roster table is where 'mapping belief and environment onto war' becomes visible.
- **The 1960 era is just the last rows of the same table** - the engine-parity contract from BL-272 made concrete.

## Open questions

1. How many era bands for the first cut? (Lean: four - classical / medieval-equivalent / gunpowder / industrial - enough turnover to test transitions without authoring forty unit types.)
2. Horses: the one material with no current signal at all (no pasture/domesticable-clade axis - BL-217's clades item was folded). Named substitution candidate: grassland share of the province window.
3. Diffusion: does a roster row spread to neighbours over time (gunpowder did not stay Chinese), and if so is contact-based diffusion a BL-271 sim mechanic or a table property? (Lean: sim mechanic - diffusion along trade/war contact is more honest and nearly free once the sim has a contact graph.)

## Military design session rulings (2026-08-07, Ben)

- **Era-keying lives in the roster only.** Verbs (BL-314) stay era-invariant; one verb precondition points at this table’s derivation. Honours combat.hpp’s era-blindness.
- **The roster artifact exists**: `Project-Rival/docs/ai/UNITS.json` (Rival-authored draft, 2026-08-07) — four era bands (classical / medieval / gunpowder / industrial, the filing lean ratified), 17 unit types, 7 doctrine presets over BL-272’s doctrine_row shape, availability derived from endowment classes + industrialisation year. Lands into Io explicitly with this item, never by silent merge.
- **Open question 2 (horses) resolved by named substitution**: grassland share of the province window, flagged in the rows that use it.
- **Open question 3 (diffusion) lean carried**: sim mechanic along the contact graph, noted on the matchlock_foot row; owned by BL-271.
- type_power_mod values are authored by judgement; calibrate against BL-271 sweep evidence when the sim runs.

## Landing contract ruled 2026-08-09 (NR-080, Ben)

Two rosters exist: the shipped engine table (src/world/unit_roster.{hpp,cpp}, 19 rows, endowment-window gates, no doctrine) and the Rival draft (Project-Rival/docs/ai/UNITS.json, 17 types, 7 doctrine presets, named_substitutions). Ruling: MERGE DELIBERATELY (option C). Reconcile row by row into the engine table — the gate mechanism is the keeper — port the doctrine presets (combat.cpp's doctrine_row is the empty socket) and the named_substitutions, and record per row which source it came from. This merge IS this item's landing; mark BL-274 complete when it lands. Neither roster simply wins.

items.title: The history sweep - run the 0-2000 CE sim over a seed spread of earth-like worlds and report the distributions the philosophy is tuned against (BL-210's batch-sweep payload)
items.summary: BL-210's one remaining scope item is the batch-sweep extension, and this gives it its real payload: sweep N seeds of earth-like generation through the full 0-2000 CE sim (BL-271) and report DISTRIBUTIONS - hegemony formation rate, war frequency and lethality, ideology mix at epoch, industrialisation onset spread, record-loss (lacunae) rates, population trajectories. Ben, 2026-08-02: 'Once generation produces a spread of earth-like planets, we can refine the crucial philosophical development of our worlds by getting tons of examples which go from 0 CE to 2000 CE.' The sweep is HOW the campaign premise's philosophical claims stop being assertions: BL-224's non-hegemony becomes a measured rate to tune toward, and BL-223's averted rupture gets designed against a thousand simulated near-ruptures instead of lore. Ben has explicitly welcomed hard failure cases ('if a problem becomes very hard to solve, I will be fascinated') - so the sweep reports the ugly distributions honestly rather than tuning them away before he sees them.

items.title: Mediterranean rift sea - a continental rift basin floods into an enclosed sea on ~90% of worlds, with a small-sea floor so a Rome-like start is never impossible
items.summary: Ben (2026-08-03): a near-Mediterranean structure - an inland sea enclosed by land - should be almost inevitable (~90% of seeds), while the remaining worlds where forming 'something like Rome' is HARD stay interesting; it must never be impossible to try. Measured baseline (tools/verify/mediterranean_sweep.cpp, 500 seeds): an enclosed sea >=300 tiles exists in only 44% of seeds today.

items.title: Era -1 military strategy - deterministic campaign-level decision-making for the Rome-sandbox nations (where armies go and why), above BL-272's battle resolution
items.summary: Filed at Ben's request (2026-08-03), same session as BL-276 (Mediterranean rift sea). BL-272 resolves a battle once armies meet; nothing yet decides WHERE armies go, what a nation is trying to take, or when it sues for peace. The Era -1 sim (BL-271) needs that strategic layer for its 2000-year wars to produce believable territorial history - and the new near-inevitable Mediterranean makes naval/littoral strategy (a Rome: control the inland sea's coasts) a live concern, not a corner case.
items.design:
## Intent (design-owed)

The campaign-level tier above BL-272 (battle resolution): per year-tick, each Era -1 nation picks military objectives and commits manpower. Everything deterministic and mechanical - this is the sandbox for the nation AI, not an LLM seam.

Questions the design must settle:

1. **Objective selection** - what a nation wants: adjacent rich provinces (farm_q), securing coasts of an enclosed sea (the BL-276 Mediterranean as a strategic prize - a Rome is a nation that closes the ring), punishing a raider, survival. Scored deterministically from province/nation state; no dice-as-strategy (checkpoint-class draws only where BL-217's mechanism applies).
2. **Force commitment** - how much of the BL-273 manpower stock to raise and where to send it; interaction with attrition and the self-limiting manpower loop so overreach collapses on its own (the hegemony-stall behaviour BL-224 wants emergent).
3. **Sea crossings** - does Era -1 strategy get naval movement across the inland sea, or coasts-only? The Mediterranean prize argues for at least a crude crossing cost; a full naval layer is almost certainly out of scope.
4. **Peace and consolidation** - when a war ends, and what territory transfer looks like against BL-218's province model; feeds BL-275's sweep metrics (war frequency, hegemony rates).
5. **Doctrine choice** - whether a nation's culture/creed leans it toward BL-272 doctrine rows (forge-god cultures fielding aggressive doctrine), reusing the existing creed data rather than new authored tables.

Scope guard: strategy for the ERA -1 SANDBOX nations only - the 1960 game's nation behaviour and the corporate AI opponent (BL-054/BL-199 arc) are explicitly untouched; the standing-rules AI-faction prohibition keeps applying to the main era.

## Naming constraint (Ben, 2026-08-03)

This item is filed off a real-history analogy ("use Rome as a sandbox"). Under the standing
rule added the same day (io-standing-rules § Terms & docs; GENERATION_STRATEGY § Real history
in, invented names out), that analogy is a **mechanism** reference only.

What this item takes from Rome: campaign-season structure, supply radii, how a frontier stalls,
how fast a hegemony forms, what makes a littoral power. What it must never take: a proper noun.
Every nation, province, city and commander the sim produces is named from the seeded sci-fi /
fantasy template banks, and the phoneme tables must not read as recognisably Latin — a name a
player can place as "the Roman one" has failed however good the mechanism under it.

Io's existing rule that Rome is *calibration reference, not content* already said this for the
mil-sim; it now applies to the whole Era −1 arc.

items.title: Io MCP server — expose the blackboard export, action dictionary and corp-command seam over the Model Context Protocol so any agent runtime can play
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03, on reading the public-field research (AI_OPPONENT.md § 10): "We can use MCP." The wrapper NR-040 was groping for. Io already has all three legs of the word interface — BL-206's blackboard export (read), BL-270's action dictionary (meaning), corp_command (write); MCP is the standard socket that turns them into something any agent runtime drives. Ships no HTTP client and no API key inside ProjectIo.exe — the server is a separate local process, and with nothing attached the game is byte-identical to today. Model-agnostic by construction, which is the whole point: the same server serves a cloud frontier model generating traces (BL-279) and the small local model those traces produce. VERSION GOAL v0.1.1 (Ben, 2026-08-03, NR-044): the server touches no simulation code, and its whole value is enabling a first real text-driven play attempt — landing it early is the "try it cheaply before designing more" lesson NR-040 already taught once. BL-279 (corpus) stays v0.2.0; it cannot start until traces exist.

items.title: AI trace corpus — log cloud play as input/output pairs and build the fine-tuning dataset for a small local model
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03: "Cloud usage is just going to be finding tons of input and output sets, for when we fine tune a smaller model of our own." The runtime target is a SMALL LOCAL model; cloud inference is a corpus generator and never a shipped dependency. A frontier model plays Io through BL-278's MCP server; every decision is logged as the pair that produced it — blackboard state + dictionary slice in, corp_command + rationale out — and those pairs become the supervised fine-tuning set. CivAgent's data-flywheel pattern and Richelieu's no-human-data self-play, on a sim whose deterministic seeds generate the scenarios for free (§ 3).
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-03 (Ben's steer + the § 10 research sweep).

## Why this is tractable rather than speculative

Three numbers from the research (AI_OPPONENT.md § 10c.6–7):

- A complete Civ V game cost `gpt-oss-120b` **20.35M input / 555k output tokens**. Read twice:
  per-tick cloud inference is not a shipping architecture, AND one game yields ~555k output
  tokens of decision trace. A few hundred logged games is a serious supervised corpus.
- Reported distillation results in this class: a **1.7B specialist beating a 744B frontier model
  on its target task**; Llama-3.2-3B going 0.76% → ~55% on GSM8K from frontier traces; 7B/8B SFT
  reaching 60% accuracy in ~1,000 steps on a card-selection task. On-task specialists beat
  generalists — which is the whole bet.
- The bar to clear is **not high**: Vox Deorum's open-weight models matched a tuned algorithmic
  4X AI (97.5% vs 97.3% survival) with a simple prompt and NO fine-tuning. The fine-tune's job
  is to get a SMALL model to that bar, not past it. Superhuman play is explicitly not the target
  and would regress the § "The goal" statement.

## The pipeline

1. **Play** — a frontier model drives Io through BL-278's MCP server across a spread of seeds
   (§ 3's benchmark seed-set is the natural sampling frame: body/terrain/market diversity).
2. **Log** — one record per decision: `{seed, tick, corp, state_slice, dictionary_slice,
   command, rationale, result}`. The record is simultaneously the training pair, the replay
   artifact, and the legibility surface — same artifact, three uses (§ 6's triple-duty argument,
   extended).
3. **Filter** — the validator is already built and free: `corp_command_result`'s typed
   rejections mechanically identify every trace containing an illegal or invalid command. The
   published recipe's "rule-based validators for format, schema compliance and novelty" is, for
   Io, mostly just this.
4. **Expand** (optional, per the published recipe) — have the teacher generate in-domain
   synthetic variants around the collected traces before SFT.
5. **Fine-tune and evaluate** — the small model is scored on BL-204's seed-set skill harness,
   the same goldens the utility core answers to. A local model that cannot hold solvency across
   the benchmark seeds has not passed, whatever a held-out loss says.

## Open, deliberately

- **Which base model.** Depends on what runs acceptably on Ben's machine at the time; the
  interface is model-agnostic by BL-278's construction, so this is a late decision, not an
  early one.
- **Corpus size.** Set empirically — collect, fine-tune, measure on BL-204, collect more.
- **Whether traces should also come from the deterministic utility core (BL-202/203).** Free to
  generate and unlimited, but caps the student at the teacher's skill (the behavioural-cloning
  ceiling, § 1 Area 3). Likely useful as bulk coverage under a thinner layer of frontier traces;
  not settled.

## Not in scope

The MCP server itself (BL-278). Any claim that the fine-tuned model ships in v0.2.0 — this item
delivers the corpus and the pipeline; whether the resulting model becomes the shipped opponent
is a later call measured against BL-204.

## Rescoped 2026-08-08 (Ben's ruling, NR-094, AI_OPPONENT.md § 10g)

The corpus this item collects no longer targets an action-emitting model. Per the C-route feasibility note's recommendation (docs/ai/LANGUAGE_POLICY_FEASIBILITY.md) and Ben's ruling adopting it: Stage A/B (corp_ai.cpp's scored-utility core) stays the action generator indefinitely -- distilling it can only reproduce it, at a legibility and determinism cost, with no skill upside. This item's corpus now trains **BL-334's Stage C dialogue layer** instead: bootstrap from corp_ai.cpp's own decision ring (free, no cloud spend) first, per the note's § 9 instruction, before spending any cloud budget. Cloud play through BL-278's MCP server is still valuable, but as a research/spectacle use of the server (an external agent playing a corp interactively), not as this item's primary corpus source -- and never as a source of corp_command-emission traces to fine-tune toward.

items.title: Negotiated tax rate — the chartered corporation bargains its rate with its home nation, making Tax a real lever with a diegetic story
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03 (NR-024): overturns the read-only-Tax call I took. A corporation cannot legislate for itself — that was the objection, and it stands — but a CHARTERED corporation can negotiate its rate with the nation that chartered it. That keeps Ben's original BL-171/BL-155 intent (Tax as a deliberate player trade-off) AND makes it coherent, and it fits the chartered-corporation identity the history ladder (BL-223) is building toward. It would also make Tax the first place diplomacy touches the economy — a bridge the game does not otherwise have before the BL-094 nation pivot.
items.design:
DESIGN OWED. Ben's steer (NR-024, 2026-08-03) is the shape, not the mechanism.

**The premise.** The player is a chartered corporation. Its tax rate is not something it enacts
and not something simply imposed on it — it is the standing term of a charter, and terms are
negotiated. The Budget ledger's Tax control therefore becomes a real lever again, but what it
sets is a *negotiating position*, not a rate.

**What needs designing.**

- **What the nation wants in return.** A lower rate has to cost something the nation values —
  candidates: guaranteed supply of a resource, a floor on domestic employment, exclusivity
  (no selling to a named rival), or accepting a cap/zoning law elsewhere in BL-155's ten.
  Without a counterparty cost this is a free money dial, which is the failure mode to avoid.
- **Where the negotiation happens.** BL-155's law surface, the corp chat log (BL-205, § 7's
  legible-messaging principle), or a dedicated charter panel. The chat route is attractive —
  it makes the first diplomacy visible in the medium the design already chose for it.
- **What the nation's willingness depends on.** Its political character (NATION_GENERATION),
  how much of its economy the corp represents, and its own fiscal position.
- **Renegotiation cadence.** Standing term with periodic review, or player-initiated at a cost?
- **The BL-094 interaction.** When the player pivots to nation, they end up on the *other* side
  of this table. The design should be written so that flip is a role swap, not a rewrite.

**Interim state.** Tax stays as BL-171 shipped it, read-only against the home nation's regime,
until this lands. That is honest — it is what a corporation with an un-negotiated charter has.

**Not in scope.** The rest of BL-155's ten laws; those stay nation-enacted with the corporation
as subject. This item carves out exactly one negotiated term.

## PARTIALLY SETTLED 2026-08-08 (Ben)

- **Negotiation surface: BL-155's Laws surface.** Tax stays where the other nine laws already
  live — a control on the Laws ledger — rather than moving to the chat log or a new charter
  panel. Simplest read: the corp sees every law, negotiated or enacted, in one place.
- **Renegotiation cadence: player-initiated, at a cost.** The player can reopen negotiation any
  time, but it costs something (time, standing, a fee — the fee mechanism itself is still open).
  Chosen over a standing-term/periodic-review model for the extra player agency.
- **Counterparty cost — still open, explicitly parked.** Ben declined to pick among the four
  candidates (resource supply guarantee, employment floor, exclusivity, cap/zoning law) this
  pass. This is the load-bearing piece — without it the rate is a free money dial, the exact
  failure mode the design already flagged — so **the item stays `design-owed`** until it's
  settled, even though the other two questions resolved.
- The BL-094 role-swap note and the nation's-willingness factors (political character, economic
  weight, fiscal position) are untouched by this pass — still open, not yet even framed as
  choices.

items.title: Retire the History ledger’s Tiles view — History becomes Story + Chain, two views about how the world came to be
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03 (NR-020): retire the view outright rather than rename it. With the per-tile table gone, the tab labelled 'Tiles' held a Buildings list and a Market table — neither a tile, and neither history. A current-state view never belonged in a HISTORY ledger; both its sections have better homes that already exist.

items.title: Trade-route history entries: log both endpoints so a body-scoped filter sees a new route from either side
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03 (NR-030): overturns my leave-as-is call. A newly established trade route is a two-body event, but `world_history_entry` carries one body tag; I tagged the destination and named both endpoints in the narration text, which meant a future 'show everything that happened at body X' filter would miss the route for its SOURCE body. Ben's call: push two entries, one tagged per endpoint.

items.title: Constrain corp asset placement to the home province, so the province decides WHERE a corporation is and not only WHAT it is
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-03 (NR-035): close the gap between BL-219's design claim and what shipped. The design says a corporation's focus follows 'the industrialisation history of the province it is anchored to'; as built, the corp picks a home province and derives its focus from it, but Pass 3 still places its starting holdings with the old nation-wide focus-scored anchor search. The province decides what the corp is; it does not yet decide where it is.
