items.title: A tile carries several buildings of any type, not just several extraction sites (answers BL-193 deferred question)
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-10: "pivot on the design philosophy that a tile is one building, and redesign the building management item to allow multiple buildings." Lifts the capacity-1 rule for non-extraction building types - which is exactly the question BL-193 (building stacks) explicitly deferred rather than answered. Enables the clustering BL-365 needs to saturate a world without carpeting it.
items.design:
### Correcting the premise first

Ben's framing was "pivot on the design philosophy that a tile is one building". **That is already
not the rule**, and this item should not be written as though it were. `placement_rules.cpp`
§ `stack_capacity`:

```
if (type != building_type::extraction_site)
    return 1;
const float richness = tc.resource_deposit[target];
return max(1, richness / k_richness_per_site);   // 1-5 by richness
```

and `buildings_on_tile` counts per `(tile, type, target)`. So one tile **already** takes several
iron sites plus several coal sites plus one processor plus one port plus one hub. What is
capacity-1 is every **non-extraction** type - which is the exact half BL-193 deferred: "Whether
processors stack on land, workforce or road tier is a separate question, deferred by BL-193 rather
than answered by it."

**So this item answers BL-193's deferred question. It is a completion, not a pivot.**

### Why it matters to BL-365, beyond Ben asking for it

Saturation needs a lot of buildings, and Kepler's land is a fraction of its 15,120 tiles.
One-building-per-tile would spread industry as a uniform carpet. Multi-building tiles let it
**cluster** around population and deposits - an industrial district rather than a lawn. Clustering
is what makes a saturated world legible instead of noisy, so this is a legibility item as much as a
capacity one.

### The design question BL-193 actually left open

What bounds a non-extraction stack? Extraction has a natural bound (deposit richness). A processor
has none. The three candidates BL-193 named:

- **Land** - a flat per-tile ceiling. Simplest; says nothing interesting.
- **Workforce** - the stack is bounded by what the body's population can staff. Ties into a shipped
  system (workforce contention already throttles an over-built corp uniformly) and makes the bound
  diegetic.
- **Road tier** - the tile's logistics capacity bounds what can sit on it. Ties into roads
  (BL-146-149) and makes infrastructure investment raise the ceiling.

**Recommendation: workforce, with road tier as a modifier.** It reuses two shipped systems, gives
the player a lever (build population / build roads to raise the cap), and produces the clustering
BL-365 wants without a magic number. **Not settled - Ben's call.**

### The output-decay question

Extraction stacks pay `0.8^(k-1)` per site, because they share one deposit. Processors do not share
a deposit, so the same decay has no physical justification. Whether a processor stack decays at all
is part of this design.

### 2026-08-11 update - stack bound resolved

Ben: capped by terrain type, and a tile that accumulates enough buildings TRANSFORMS to a new "urban" terrain type. This is a new mechanic, not a simple numeric bound - it introduces a tile-composition transition at runtime (today's terrain is set once at generation) and a new `terrain_composition` value. Follow-on design work needed before this is buildable: the building-count threshold per starting terrain type, whether the transform is reversible (a tile that loses buildings ever reverts?), what "urban" terrain does to deposits/ambient-resource guarantee (TILES.md), and whether it changes tile stat/movement rules the way other composition values do. Files gain docs/economy/TILES.md and the terrain_composition enum (likely src/world/components.hpp or tile-adjacent header).

### 2026-08-11 second update - the urban-transform mechanic, designed

Ben's answer widened the question: the bound is **terrain-type capacity**, and a tile that fills
its capacity **transforms** to a new `urban` terrain-composition value. This is consistent with
TILES.md's own framing — "a fixed character set at world generation... does not change during play
except through deliberate player development" — the transform IS that deliberate-development
exception, not a violation of the fixed-at-generation rule.

**Scope note:** this only bounds *non-extraction* stacking (processors, ports, hubs, admin,
amenity, military base — the half BL-193 deferred and this item answers). Extraction stacking stays
richness-bound as shipped; it is a separate axis and untouched here.

**The cap table (authored, per starting composition — first cut, tunable data not a hardcoded rule):**

| Composition | Non-extraction cap | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Grassland, Forest, Wetland | 6 | Habitable; already the settlement-favoured compositions (POPULATION.md) |
| Tundra | 3 | Marginal habitability |
| Barren, Rocky, Regolith, Metallic | 4 | Industrial-friendly, low habitability ceiling |
| Volcanic, Icy | 2 | Hostile; TILES.md already gives these the lowest habitability ceiling |
| Ocean | n/a, exempt | Already capacity-1/no-buildings; this item does not touch water tiles |

**The transform, once capacity is reached:**

- Composition flips to a new **`urban`** value in `terrain_composition` (12th value). One-way,
  never reverts — matches TILES.md's "fixed... except through deliberate development" framing, and
  keeps the mechanic simple (no decay/abandonment modelling, which is out of scope here).
- Urban's own non-extraction cap is high (first cut: 12) — soft-bounded in practice by workforce
  contention (the shipped system), not by this cap.
- **No new extraction or ambient-resource placement on an urban tile** — the ground is built over.
  Extraction sites already standing when the transform fires are grandfathered and keep operating
  (deliberately not retconning existing player investment).
- Urban gets the **High** habitability ceiling (matches the settlement-favoured compositions it
  supersedes) and a build-cost/logistics discount reflecting established infrastructure — reuses
  the existing `landform_logistics_cost` multiplier mechanism rather than inventing a second cost
  axis; exact multiplier is an implementation-time tuning value, not a design commitment.
- Fires identically for player, rival and background corps — deterministic, no new exception to the
  standing rules (the transform is a mechanical consequence of building count, not an agency grant).

**Implementation shape (for the promoted task, not committed yet):**
- New `terrain_composition::urban` enum value, `src/world/components.hpp`.
- `stack_capacity` (`placement_rules.cpp`) reads a per-composition cap table for non-extraction
  types instead of the flat `return 1`.
- A transform check (e.g. `maybe_transform_to_urban(tile)`) runs after non-extraction placement,
  flips `terrain_composition` when the cap is hit. Determinism: pure function of tile state, no RNG.
- TILES.md gains the urban row (composition table, ambient-resource table exclusion, habitability)
  and the cap table above **once this lands**, per the standing authority time-slice rule — not
  before.

**Still open, left for the promoted task rather than blocking design:** whether the player gets an
explicit notification/log line when a tile transforms (a UI polish question, not a mechanic one),
and the exact urban logistics-cost discount value (a tuning number, set at implementation and
measured, not authored here).
items.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. terrain_composition::urban (12th value, components.hpp). non_extraction_stack_cap per-composition table + non_extraction_buildings_on_tile aggregate counter + maybe_transform_to_urban one-way transform, placement_rules.{hpp,cpp}; wired into construct_building (construction.cpp) after a non-extraction placement. can_place refuses new extraction/ambient placement on an urban tile (pre-existing extraction sites grandfathered); transform raises tile habitability to >= 0.80, never lowers it. presentation.cpp/hex_render.cpp gain the urban name+colour. New multi_building_tile_harness (26/26 PASS): cap table, aggregate cross-type occupancy, transform firing on the 6th mixed-type placement, urban's own higher cap, extraction refusal post-transform, grandfathering, habitability floor (both directions), and extraction stacking left unchanged. construction_harness/determinism_harness/world_audit/construction_gate_harness/buildings_rework_harness rerun clean, zero regression. Full ProjectIo build clean. Not built: the per-composition build-cost/logistics discount and the transform notification/log line, both named in the design as implementation-time tuning values, not committed here. docs/economy/TILES.md gains § Urban transform; docs/economy/PRODUCTION.md's non-extraction-stacking paragraph updated from “deferred” to “answered”.

items.title: The building-management surface handles a tile holding several buildings of several types
items.summary: BL-229 (building management in Menu Space) is complete at v0.1.10 and put management into the construction element format. Ben, 2026-08-10: "redesign the building management item to allow multiple buildings." Once BL-366 lifts the capacity-1 rule a tile can hold a heterogeneous set, and the surface has to make that readable and individually actionable.
items.design:
Follows BL-366. Once the capacity-1 rule is lifted for non-extraction types, a tile can hold a
heterogeneous set - several extraction stacks against different deposits, several processors, plus
infrastructure - and BL-229's surface has to make that readable and individually actionable.

### Open questions

- **Flat list or grouped by stack?** `stack_members` already thinks in terms of `(type, target)`
  stacks; the surface could mirror that grouping or present a flat list of buildings.
- **What does clicking the tile select, versus clicking a specific marker?** SELECTION.md's
  single-click-selects / double-click-navigates model has to extend to a tile with eight things on
  it.
- **How does the on-canvas marker render a tile with eight buildings without becoming a blob?**
  ICONS.md owns the glyph vocabulary and would need a "stack of N" treatment.

### Required alongside

`question_log.json` entries - the question/why pair is mandatory on every changed UI surface
(BL-260), and this changes one materially.

### 2026-08-11 update - all three questions resolved from shipped precedent

**Grouped by stack, not a flat list.** `stack_members` (placement_rules) already groups by
`(type, target)`; the surface mirrors that grouping rather than inventing a second one. Each
stack gets one row/header (e.g. "Extraction: Iron Ore x3", "Processing: Steel Mill x2") with its
members underneath - consistent with BL-229's existing construction-ledger format, extended one
level rather than replaced.

**Click model: tile selects the aggregate, a specific on-canvas marker selects its stack.**
Extends SELECTION.md's single-click-selects / double-click-navigates model rather than replacing
it: clicking empty tile ground (or the tile's base glyph) selects the tile as today, showing the
grouped stack list above; clicking a specific building marker within that tile selects that
stack directly, scrolling the Selection panel to it. No new interaction primitive - this is the
same click-resolves-to-nearest-marker logic Selection already uses to distinguish a body from
its markers on the Solar canvas (CANVASES.md § shared layout).

**On-canvas marker: dominant-stack glyph + a count badge, reusing the survey badge's k/N
convention.** ICONS.md's survey badge already overlays a small text count (`k/N` region
progress) on a base glyph rather than growing the glyph itself with count - BL-367 reuses exactly
that pattern instead of inventing a "blob" shape. The marker renders the tile's highest-value
stack's glyph (extraction pip, processor icon, etc.) plus a small "+N" badge when the tile holds
more than one stack, lower-right per the survey/activity badge offset convention (ICONS.md
already staggers multiple badges on one marker to avoid overlap). No new glyph shape needed;
ICONS.md gains the badge's exact offset/size spec when this lands.

Required alongside: `question_log.json` entries per BL-260, as the item's summary already notes.
items.resolution: 2026-08-12 -- complete. construction_panel.cpp's draw_selected_section groups a tile's buildings by (type, target) stack (tile_stacks()/draw_tile_stack_list()), mirroring placement_rules::stack_members' own grouping rather than inventing a second one -- a tile with exactly one building still routes straight to its detail (zero extra clicks), more than one shows the grouped list first, and a '<- this tile's buildings' back link returns from a drilled-into stack. selection_panel.cpp's Manage button and body_surface_canvas.cpp's on-canvas marker click (both the hit-zone and the missed-marker fallback) now count buildings-per-tile before deciding whether to jump straight to the single building or fall through to the tile -- previously both silently grabbed an arbitrary first match from an unordered_map. The on-canvas marker gained a '+N' count badge (dominant-stack glyph unchanged, no new glyph shape), staggered lower-right past the existing BL-090 corp-identity tag, reusing the k/N text-overlay idiom the Solar-canvas survey badge already uses. Docs: SELECTION.md gained a Multi-building tiles section, ICONS.md catalogues the badge, question_log.json's construction_panel/selection_panel entries carry BL-367. Verified: ProjectIo builds clean, launches without crash. NOT verified: a live screenshot of an actual multi-building tile (NR-173) -- likely to surface naturally in the next live session given BL-365's background firms.

items.title: Population centres generate real, clearing market demand - the half of the substrate that is genuinely demand
items.summary: Removing the substrate (BL-365) removes two things at once: fake supply, which BL-365 replaces with real firms, and per-capita demand, which has no replacement unless population centres actually consume. This item owns the demand half, and carries a known shipped bug: the population agri-demand stub is written into markets and then zero-reset before clearing every tick, so it never lands.
items.design:
### Why it is separate from BL-365

Removing the substrate removes two things at once: fake supply (which BL-365 replaces with real
firms) and per-capita demand (which has no replacement unless population centres actually consume).
Splitting them keeps each independently verifiable, and the demand half is the one with a known bug
already attached.

### The known bug it must fix

MARKETS.md § Known limitations records it: the population agri demand stub never reaches clearing.
`run_economy_step`'s population pass writes `agricultural_produce` demand directly into markets, but
`clear_markets` zero-resets demand before accumulating - so the write is erased the same tick. The
real pull today is the substrate basket.

**Take the substrate away without fixing this and population demand is zero, not restored.** That is
the failure mode this item exists to prevent, and it is why this lands before BL-365 rather than
after.

### Scope

Generalise the erased agri stub into a real per-centre basket across the tradeable set, written at
the right point in the clearing order (after the reset, alongside the other demand sources), with
the price elasticity the substrate basket already models moved onto it.

### Open question

Habitability goods (clean water, consumer goods, medical supplies) are what a population *should*
consume, and none of them exist as `resource_type` values. Either population demand is restricted to
the goods that do exist (food_rations, agricultural_produce, water, refined_fuel), or this item
grows a resource tranche of its own - which would then want reading against BL-340's admission rule
(a resource must have a consumer or be a terminal object; no orphans).

### 2026-08-11 update - resource-tranche question resolved: grow it now

**Ben: add the habitability-goods tranche now**, rather than restricting population demand to the
four resources that already exist. Scope, drawn from RESOURCES.md's already-authored (but
un-modelled) habitability table:

- **Three new `resource_type` values land: Clean Water, Consumer Goods, Medical Supplies.**
  Building Materials and Utilities are explicitly OUT of this item's scope - Building Materials
  feeds construction cost (a different consumption path, PRODUCTION.md's concern, not population
  demand), and Utilities is already modelled as an abstracted budget cost with no resource
  identity of its own (RESOURCES.md is explicit on this). Only the three that population centres
  actually consume as tradeable goods are in scope.
- **Each gets a producing building** (Water Treatment Plant, Consumer Goods Factory,
  Pharmaceutical Lab per RESOURCES.md's table), satisfying BL-340's admission rule (a resource
  must have a consumer AND a producer, no orphans) on both ends: population centres are the
  consumer, the new building is the producer. Recipe inputs per the existing table - water for
  Clean Water; food_rations + refined goods for Consumer Goods; chemical + agricultural outputs
  for Medical Supplies - exact recipe quantities are an implementation-time tuning value, not
  authored here, matching how every other recipe in the prototype is handled.
- **Supply comes from BL-365's generation-till-target-fraction model, same as any other good** -
  this item does not hand-place these three buildings; BL-365's background-firm generation builds
  them like any other production building once the recipe/building types exist. This item's own
  scope is the resource_type values, the three building_type values + recipes, and the population
  demand basket read; BL-365 supplies the firms that produce them.
- **Save-format consequence**: three new resource_type enum values grow every per-resource array
  (sized by resource_count, already the additive pattern the enum has followed - see BL-107's
  version-header note on this being a live, not hypothetical, step now). No format-breaking
  change, purely additive.
- Files gain `docs/economy/PRODUCTION.md` (building/recipe tables), `docs/economy/RESOURCES.md`
  (flip the "None of this table exists" banner for the three landing values), and
  `src/world/components.hpp` (enum growth) alongside the item's existing file scope.
items.resolution: 2026-08-11 — complete. Generalised the BL-190 flat agricultural_produce-only population demand stub into a real, price-elastic, multi-resource basket (population_demand_params, economy.population_demand in Lua), same elastic shape as the BL-078 nation-substrate model but population-only (no supply term). Discovered in passing: the "known bug" the item's own design cited (population demand erased by clear_markets' reset) had already been fixed by BL-190 (2026-07-31) — the design prose was stale; MARKETS.md's Known-limitations bullet repeating the same stale claim corrected in this pass. Grew resource_type by three (39 -> 42): clean_water, consumer_goods, medical_supplies, per RESOURCES.md's habitability table — Building Materials and Utilities deliberately left out (construction-cost path / abstracted budget cost, not population demand). Three new recipes on the generic processing_facility (scripts/recipes.lua ids 14-16, no new building_type values): clean_water (water->clean_water), consumer_goods (food_rations+steel->consumer_goods), medical_supplies (water+agricultural_produce->medical_supplies) — base prices in world_gen.lua. New population_demand_harness R4 (elasticity + multi-resource + untradeable-skip, 4/4 PASS) and new habitability_tranche_harness (9/9 PASS: production, off-ceiling pricing, population demand reaching the market for all three goods). Full ProjectIo build clean; econ_harness/econ_stability/resource_chain_harness/determinism_harness/construction_harness/world_audit/construction_gate_harness/buildings_rework_harness/multi_building_tile_harness all rerun clean. ai_skill_harness golden-band drift investigated (stash-and-rerun against the pre-BL-368 baseline) and found to predate this item — BL-366 alone had already moved it from 5 to 8 failures, unnoticed at that landing; filed as NR-169 rather than silently re-blessed. Not built (named per Rule 0c): the undersupply-effects feedback into habitability/workforce efficiency/growth — the demand signal now moves prices but does not yet feed back into the population model; that stays open follow-on. docs/economy/RESOURCES.md, PRODUCTION.md and MARKETS.md updated (clearing-tick step list, Known-limitations correction, habitability tranche tables).

items.title: The warm start runs 80 ticks but consumes no in-game time - decide whether that is right
items.summary: Filed from the 2026-08-10 warm-start change (pre_game_ticks 12 -> 80). Ben framed it as "start the game running from perhaps 1956 or so", which reads as the campaign beginning earlier. It does not: app::start_new_game runs the ticks and then rebases the clock, so the warm start costs no calendar time and play still opens at epoch_year (1960).
items.design:
### The question

`app::start_new_game` runs `pre_game_ticks` and then **rebases the clock**, so the warm start
consumes no in-game time and play still opens at `epoch_year` (1960). The world is generated *at*
1960 state and then ticked forward 20 years, with the result relabelled as the 1960 opening
position.

Is the warm start:

**(a)** a settling pass on a 1960 world, with the calendar correctly untouched, or
**(b)** genuinely the years 1940-1960, in which case generation should produce a **1940** world and
the clock should advance to 1960 during it?

(b) is the more coherent story and much the larger change - it would interact with BL-271's Era -1
history sim, which already runs 0->1960 and would need to stop at 1940 and hand over. (a) is what is
built and is defensible: the pre-game history is a fiction that produces a plausible opening
position, not a simulated two decades.

### Recommendation

**(a), documented.** Say plainly in ERAS.md that the warm start is a settling pass with no calendar
meaning. Revisit only if the opening year becomes player-visible or configurable - which the New
World wizard (STARTUP.md) could plausibly make it.

### 2026-08-11 - settled

Ben: (a) - the warm start is a settling pass with no calendar meaning; play still opens at epoch_year (1960). Action: add a short note to docs/economy/ERAS.md stating the warm start consumes no in-game time and is not a simulated 1940->1960 history. Light-mode doc change, no code change needed.

items.summary: Filed from the 2026-08-11 notes session. Ben asked whether a leader system could be built so the player feels a personal connection to the public/private corp they play as - a named figure standing in for the corp, distinct from the corp itself.

Ben asked whether there is room for public acquisitions - the player buying into or taking over an existing public corporation - as an alternate route into new capability versus building from scratch.

items.title: Lens-keyed selection - the active lens declares what a click selects
items.summary: Ben's idea, 2026-08-12 (NR-176, answered the same day). Selection is lens-blind today: the Planetary canvas resolves a click by a fixed marker priority (building > market_centre > tile) and overlay_mode feeds only the draw pass. Make the active lens declare the selection subject instead, so what the player is looking at is what a click grabs.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **option 1 - the lens REPLACES the selection subject** while it is active, rather than merely promoting it up the existing hit-test priority.

Mapping (the lens names its subject):
- Resource -> the deposit under the cursor
- Country -> the nation owning the tile
- Corporation -> the corp owning the tile
- Market -> the market centre serving the tile
- none -> today's behaviour, building > market_centre > tile

OPEN CONSTRAINT carried from NR-176, and the main thing to settle before building: three lenses have no tile-grid subject at all - **Reach**, **Supply-routes** and **Scarcity** are body-level or edge-level. Under a replace rule those lenses would make clicks inert. Each must therefore either name a subject explicitly (Reach / Supply-routes: the body, or the route edge under the cursor; Scarcity: the market) or opt out and keep the default priority. Enumerate all 14 overlay_mode values and give each an answer - a lens with no declared subject is a bug, not a default.

This touches three docs beyond the code. SELECTION.md owns the click model (single-click selects, double-click navigates) and must record that the *subject* is now lens-conditional while the *gesture* is not. LENSES.md gains a subject column in its roster table. ACTIONS.json's canvas family is the one an AI player reads: every canvas click action's expected_output becomes conditional on the active lens, and a stale entry there misleads the AI player exactly as a stale golden misleads a visual check.

Worth doing after or alongside BL-364 (corp borders), which shares the Corporation-lens surface.

items.title: Re-point the Industry lens at real background-firm buildings
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-173. BL-365 replaced the abstract nation substrate with real background corporations, leaving tile.substrate_density (the Industry lens input) as, in its own generation comment, "purely a rendering field now" - the lens tints where background industry plausibly would sit, while the real firms are ordinary buildings elsewhere on the same map.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **option 1 - re-point the lens at the real thing.** Tint each tile by the count/output of is_background corp buildings on it, which is what the lens name has always promised and what BL-365's generated firms now make available.

The question the re-pointed lens answers is 'where is the industry I did not build?' - which Production does not quite ask, since Production is body-relative output intensity including the player's own holdings. Keeping both is therefore justified; retiring Industry in favour of Production (option 2) was the close runner-up and is the fallback if the two turn out to render near-identically in practice.

tile.substrate_density is NOT deleted (option 4 declined): it is cheap, and removing it is a save-format touch for no gain. It simply stops being this lens's input.

LENSES.md and the lens.industry entry in ACTIONS.json were corrected in the 2026-08-12 sweep to stop claiming the field injects background supply/demand into markets; both need a second pass once the lens actually reads buildings, since reason_to_select will finally be true rather than merely not-false. Re-bless the industry lens golden.

items.title: Corporation density target - about 22 private corporations per nation
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-163. Neither NATION_GENERATION.md nor GENERATION_STRATEGY.md fixed a corporation count; the premise (player + major AI as lean specialists against a saturated economy) implies many background firms but never said how many.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **~22 private corporations per nation** is the density target - above the midpoint of the 10-20 he originally floated, so read it as a crowded market rather than a cast of named rivals.

Two things this is not. It is not yet a measurement: the generator currently opens far leaner, so reaching 22/nation is a generation change, and at that density the per-tick cost of corp_ai's scored-utility evaluation over every background corp becomes the binding constraint (NR-162, the unmeasured hardware question, is the sibling - measure before scaling). And it is not a hard floor: a nation whose provinces cannot support that many firms should open leaner and say so, consistent with the NR-118 answer that focus - and by extension presence - follows the ground.

Sequencing note: this interacts with BL-365's saturation calibration. Saturation is a calibrated generation invariant, not an authored building count (NR-151), and this density target must be expressed the same way - a target the calibration aims at, not a literal per-nation loop count.

items.title: Pacing target - a skilled player reaches space in 20-40 years
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-168, and answers NR-166. Ben wanted assurance that base-game international trade reliably clears and that a player can plausibly beat Era 1 on trade alone; there was no stated invariant for this in MARKETS.md or FINANCE.md, only an implicit hope.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **a skilled player should reach space industry in about 20-40 years of game time.**

This is stronger than the question asked for, in the useful direction: it is bounded on both sides. Under ~20 years the base game is too easy and Era 0 has no weight; over ~40 it stalls, which is the failure NR-168 was actually worried about. So it is a checkable pacing target, not a reassurance.

Three pieces of work follow.

1. **Write it down.** ERAS.md is the natural home - it owns the Era 0 -> Era 1 transition and already carries the not-implemented banner. MARKETS.md and FINANCE.md should cite it rather than restate it, since what they own is the clearing behaviour that has to make the target reachable.

2. **Measure it.** This wants a headless harness (tools/verify/) that runs a competent-play approximation forward and reports the year at which Rocketry + launchpad + propellant first become affordable - the same shape as pregame_balance_harness. Beware the trap NR-156 records there: an assertion that passes off a band peg measures nothing.

3. **Only then tune.** Do not reshape prices to hit the number before the number has been measured once. Measure, then decide whether the economy or the target is wrong.

Blocked in practice on Era 1 gating being implemented at all (ERAS.md: designed, not implemented); until then a harness can measure affordability, not the actual transition.

items.title: Continent lens key floats above the always-open Selection band
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-104. BL-266 made the Selection band always-open, and the Continent lens key now permanently overlaps its corner (visible in the continents_lens_kepler_key capture).
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **the key floats above the band.** It keeps its current position and gains z-order over the always-open Selection band - it does not move to the opposite corner, and it does not dock into the minimap lens bar.

So this is a draw-order fix rather than a layout change, which is why it is difficulty 1. Check the float reads correctly against the band's own background - the key may need its own opaque backing rather than relying on the canvas behind it, which is no longer what sits underneath. Re-bless continents_lens_kepler_key.

Separate and still open: NR-104's other half, the broad golden re-bless owed after BL-266 removed the [x] dismiss control and moved [>]. That is not this item - see NR-104 and NR-130.

items.title: The mercenary contract seam — a polity pays the player's company to make a fact about the world true
items.summary: The sell side of the mercenary company, and the player's income under the 0 CE refocus (NR-177). A contract is a condition_set (BL-342, shipped) that a client polity will pay to have become true by a deadline; the player chooses what force to commit, which is what keeps it a strategy rather than a mission list. Offers are derived from history_sim's existing campaign scorer — a polity that wants a province but cannot take it alone offers it as a contract — so offers are deterministic and their fees track a value the sim already computes. Reuses BL-350's command seam, split-payment pacing and (buyer, supplier) reputation scalar, but needs its own record: procurement's resource+quantity deliverable and countdown completion cannot express 'hold this province through the season', and it needs a third terminal state (failed) distinct from cancelled.
items.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-12, at Ben's request, as the first design work of the 0 CE refocus
(NR-177). This is the item NR-177 names as *"the mercenary SELL side (who contracts you, on what
terms, win/lose consequences) has no item at all, where procurement.cpp is only the buy side."*

### What this item owns

The player's **income**. Under the refocus the player is a mercenary company — the militia ancestor
— and a mercenary company's core loop is not extraction and it is not trade. It is: **be
contracted, field force, be paid.** Every other system in the game is either what you spend that
money on or what makes fielding force expensive.

That makes this the item the refocused product stands on. BL-350 shipped the seam by which the
player **buys**; nothing yet describes the seam by which it **earns**.

### The claim to reuse — stated precisely, because the loose version is wrong

The tempting one-liner is *"a mercenary contract is BL-350's procurement contract with the player as
the supplier."* **That is wrong in the part that matters**, and stating why is what shapes the
design.

`procurement_contract` (components.hpp:499, a 40-byte save-format record) carries
`resource + quantity` as its deliverable and completes when `ticks_elapsed` reaches
`lead_time_ticks`. Both are wrong here:

- **The deliverable is not fungible.** `resource + quantity` cannot express *"hold the river
  province through the campaign season"*. There is no resource whose quantity means that.
- **Completion is not a countdown.** A procurement contract finishes when enough ticks pass. A
  mercenary contract finishes when a **fact about the world** becomes true — or fails when the
  deadline passes and it is still false.
- **Failure is a distinct outcome from cancellation.** BL-350 has cancel (you walked away, you
  forfeit the deposit). This needs *lost* (you fought, you were beaten) — the same money outcome,
  a very different reputation and narrative outcome, and the one that makes contracts risky.

So: **a sibling record, not the same record.** What genuinely transfers is three shipped things,
and they are worth having:

1. **The command seam.** Three more `corp_verb`s appended to the same enum BL-350 extended to 14
   (append-only, BL-293's convention), so the player's press and an AI's command stay one
   implementation.
2. **The split-payment pacing.** Deposit on acceptance, remainder across the term — BL-350's Q1
   answer, already tuned, already legible, already reusing BL-095's construction model.
3. **The reputation scalar.** `world::corp_reputation`, a (buyer, supplier) map, already
   serialised. A mercenary's standing with a client is exactly that object.

### The spine

> **A contract is a condition_set the client will pay to have become true, by a deadline.**

That is the design, and it is short because `condition_set` (BL-342, shipped v0.1.3) is already
generic, pure, deterministic predicate machinery — and BL-350 already evaluates one for its
embargo decline, so the precedent for using it as *contract terms* is set rather than invented.

A contract record therefore carries: the client, the company, a **success `condition_set`**, a
**deadline in ticks**, a fee, a deposit fraction, and the accrued state (`ticks_elapsed`,
`deposit_paid`). The whole variety of contract types — take this province, hold that one, break a
siege, escort a convoy, deny a road — is **authored data in the predicate**, not a type enum in
C++. Adding a contract kind is a Lua change.

This is the design's main claim to legibility and it is the same claim BL-350 made: reuse a shipped,
understood mechanism rather than invent a parallel one.

### Where offers come from — the second reuse, and the stronger one

Contracts must be *offered* by someone, and the offers must be deterministic (io-standing-rules
§ Determinism). The answer is already in the tree.

`history_sim.cpp` scores four verbs per polity per year, and one of them is **campaign** — a pure,
integer, argmax-over-bounded-candidates scorer that already decides *which neighbouring province a
polity wants and how badly* (`w_farm`, `w_ore`, `w_port`, `w_ring`, `w_dist`, `w_def`,
`w_cult`). It also already computes the **stall**: a campaign whose arriving force falls under
`stalled_supply_q` because the objective is too far or the defender too strong.

> **A contract offer is a campaign the polity wants and cannot win alone.**

Take the existing candidate scoring; where the polity's own projected force is insufficient but the
objective's value is high, it does not launch — it **offers the objective as a contract**, at a fee
derived from the value it scored. Where it can win alone, it campaigns and offers nothing.

Three things this buys, none of which needs new machinery:
- **Offers are deterministic and replayable**, because the scorer already is.
- **Offers are legible**, because the fee tracks a value the sim actually computed rather than a
  designer's table.
- **The contract market has a natural rhythm** — offers appear when the political map is under
  tension and dry up when it is settled, which is a *reason* for boom and drought rather than a
  spawn timer.

The architecture transfers; the constants do not. That is BL-271's own transfer contract, applied.

### The four questions this design has to answer

**Q1 — Does the player choose the force, or does the contract specify it?**
**The player chooses.** The contract names the *outcome* and the *fee*, never the force. This is the
single decision that keeps the item a strategy game rather than a mission list: the whole skill is
reading whether the fee covers the force the objective actually needs, and a contract that specifies
its own force has pre-solved that.

It also makes underbidding a real failure mode — take a cheap contract, send too little, lose the
fight, lose the fee *and* the standing. That is the loop's teeth.

**Q2 — What happens on failure?**
Three distinct terminal states, deliberately, against BL-350's two:
- **completed** — the predicate held before the deadline. Balance of fee paid, reputation up.
- **failed** — the deadline passed with the predicate false. Deposit forfeit, no balance, reputation
  down *harder* than cancellation. You are not paid for trying.
- **cancelled** — the player withdrew before the deadline. Deposit forfeit, reputation down, but
  less than failure. An honest early exit costs less than a rout.

Failure must be survivable, per CONCEPT.md § Stagnation as loss: there is no lose screen, and losing
a contract is a *progressive* setback. The loss vector is the spiral — reputation falls, fees on
offer fall with it, and the company can no longer afford the force that would win the contracts that
would restore it. That is bankruptcy-by-reputation, and it is the mercenary reading of CONCEPT.md's
two existing loss vectors rather than a third one.

**Q3 — Can the player hold contracts from opposed clients?**
**Yes, and nothing prevents it mechanically — but standing prices it.** Accepting a contract against
a client you also serve is legal, resolves normally, and costs reputation with the injured party on
completion. Making it *illegal* would need a faction-alignment model the game does not have and the
refocus does not want; making it *free* would delete the only interesting thing about being a
mercenary.

This is the one answer here taken on design judgement rather than derived from a shipped mechanism.
It is recorded in NR-177's family as reversible.

**Q4 — Is the contract offer public or private?**
**Private per client, visible to the player only where the activity fog already reaches** — the
existing `body_activity_visibility` tiers (BL-089, DISCOVERY.md). A polity you have never dealt
with and cannot see does not offer you work. This gives the discovery layer a second job for free
and gives reputation a *reach* dimension: standing opens the map, not just the price.

### Serialisation

A **fifth flat-binary stream** after history_log, order_book and procurement, following procurement
exactly: leading magic (`IOMC`) + version, count-prefixed records, rejection rather than
reinterpretation, a `static_assert` on the record size as the tripwire. See procurement.hpp; this
item does not restate the rationale.

The `condition_set` in the record is the one novel serialisation question — it is a structured
predicate, not a scalar. Two options at promotion: store the predicate inline, or store an index
into an authored contract-template table and keep the predicate in Lua. **Recommend the template
index**: it keeps the binary record fixed-size, it makes contract kinds data, and a save that
outlives a template-table change should reject rather than reinterpret, which the version bump
already gives.

### Scope explicitly excluded

The combat that resolves a contract (**BL-315**, conflict spine — this item states what is *at
stake*, never how a fight resolves). Unit materiel draw per tick. Multi-round fee haggling — a
contract is take-it-or-leave-it in this cut, matching BL-350's Q4 exclusion. Contracts between the
player and *another corporation* rather than a polity. Any narrative or dialogue layer.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`headless`, a new contract_harness: one contract offered by the objective scorer, accepted, paced
and completed with the fee paid in the split shape; plus one observed instance of **each** of the
three terminal states, and one determinism assertion (same seed, same offers). Written this way
because Sprint 9's `hire_unit` shipped correct and was never observed firing across five seeds
(NR-121), and BL-350's own requirement was written to stop that recurring.

items.title: Retire the circumplanetary minimap — the inset becomes a fixed max-zoom render of the player's starting base
items.summary: Under the 0 CE refocus (NR-177) space is unreachable, so the minimap's circumplanetary rung shows a place the player can never act in. Ben, 2026-08-12: turn it into 'a max zoom canvas render, fixed on the player's starting base'. The inset stops being navigation and becomes identity — a persistent close-up of your camp, which is the right readout for a mercenary company that is structurally always away from home. Cheap by reuse: BL-194 already ships a zoomed tile-neighbourhood inset in the Selection band drawing through hex_render.hpp, so this is that renderer pointed at the player's military_base tile (BL-331, landed) at kMaxZoom (20.0, body_surface_canvas.cpp:44). The minimap box must keep its rect (336x252 at 1080p) because selection_band_height is derived from minimap_height. The navigable ladder collapses with it — solar and circumplanetary get gated off rather than deleted, so Ben's DLC merge-back is a flag flip and not a revert.
items.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-12, from Ben's steer the same day. **Corrected mid-session** — the
first cut of this item read his *"change the canvas to a mini-map"* as *the minimap becomes a world
overview with a viewport rect and click-to-pan*. That was wrong. His actual meaning:

> *"I meant the circumplanetary mini-map to a max zoom canvas render, fixed on the player's starting
> base."*

Not an overview. A **fixed close-up of home**. The rest of this design is written against that.

### The problem

`canvas_level` (ui_state.hpp:16) has three rungs — `solar`, `circumplanetary`, `planetary` —
and MINIMAP.md's model is *the minimap always shows the rung one step out*. With the primary canvas
on Planetary, the minimap therefore shows **Circumplanetary**: a planet with its moons and local
space.

Under the refocus that view is dead weight. There is one body, space is unreachable, and the inset
spends 336 x 252 px of prime screen real estate showing somewhere the player can never go.

### The replacement

> The inset becomes the **Planetary canvas rendered at maximum zoom, camera locked to the player's
> starting base.**

It is not a navigation control and not an overview. It is a **standing readout of home** — what your
camp looks like right now, at full detail, while the primary canvas is somewhere else entirely.

**Why that is the right object for this game specifically.** A mercenary company is structurally
always away from home: the contracts (BL-377) are fought on someone else's ground, and the primary
canvas follows the fighting. The one thing the player has that is *theirs* is the base. Giving it
permanent screen presence makes the company feel like a company rather than a cursor, and it costs
no new interaction vocabulary at all.

It also quietly answers "what do I own" without a ledger round-trip, which is the same argument
BL-194's Selection-band neighbourhood view already won.

### Cheap by reuse — this is mostly wiring

Three shipped pieces do the work:

1. **BL-194's zoomed tile-neighbourhood view** already renders a small hex neighbourhood into an
   inset rect in the Selection band. That is this feature, pointed somewhere else.
2. **`hex_render.hpp`** is already the shared source of truth for the terrain palette
   (`terrain_colour`), the landform relief channel (`landform_relief`) and hex geometry —
   extracted precisely so the band inset and the main canvas do not diverge. A third consumer is
   what it was built for.
3. **BL-331 (landed)** seeds the player corp with one `military_base` on a home-province tile, so
   the camera target is a real entity from turn one rather than something this item must invent.

Zoom bounds are already defined: `kMaxZoom = 20.0f`, `kMinZoom ~= 0.877`
(body_surface_canvas.cpp:44-45). "Max zoom" is therefore a value, not a judgement call.

### The layout constraint — the minimap box keeps its rect

`selection_band_height = minimap_height + chrome_margin` (foldout_column.cpp:44-49), where
`minimap_width = max(336, 0.28 x min(disp_x, disp_y))` and `minimap_height = 0.75 x width`.
That is **336 x 252 px at 1920x1080** and 403 x 302 at 2560x1440.

The Selection band's height is derived from the minimap's so the bottom strip's top edge lands
exactly on the minimap's — the alignment BL-216 and BL-312 were written to fix. **Changing the
inset's contents is free; changing its rect is not.** If a later item wants it resized, the
derivation must be re-anchored first, as its own change.

### The ladder collapses with it — by GATING, not deleting

With the inset no longer showing the rung above, nothing reaches `solar` or `circumplanetary`
and the asymmetric descend-by-body / ascend-by-minimap model has no referent.

**Do not delete them.** Ben's ruling (NR-177) is *stash the space work and merge it back for DLC*,
which makes deletion the expensive path — resurrecting reverted code across months of divergence.
`canvas_level` keeps all three enumerators behind a world-level capability flag (era, or an
explicit `space_reachable`). The ancient product ships with it false; the DLC merge is a flag flip
plus content. SOLAR.md and CIRCUMPLANETARY.md then document a gated feature rather than rotting.

### The three open calls

**Q1 — Is the inset interactive at all?**
"Fixed" is explicit, so **no pan and no zoom inside it**. But a single click is nearly free and
obviously wanted: **recommend click-to-centre** — clicking the inset moves the *primary* canvas to
the base. That keeps the inset itself fixed (Ben's word) while giving "go home" a one-click home,
which a player will otherwise want within about ten minutes.

**Q2 — What is the target if the starting base is gone?**
Bases can be demolished, and a mercenary company plausibly relocates. `corporation_component`
already carries an **HQ** (BL-182 — the holding nearest the corp's holdings centroid, designated at
generation), which is defined for every corp and survives any single building's loss.
**Recommend: the starting base, falling back to the corp HQ**, so the inset always has a subject and
never renders empty.

**Q3 — Does it show live activity, or just terrain?**
**Recommend live** — units garrisoned, the building's own state, construction in progress. A static
terrain thumbnail is a screenshot; the reason to give a readout permanent screen space is that it
*changes*. This is the difference between the feature being loved and being ignored.

All three are recorded here as reversible rather than assumed settled.

### The action dictionary must move with it

Entries in the `canvas` family of ACTIONS.json are invalidated, and a stale entry misleads a
text-driven player exactly as a stale golden misleads a visual check (ACTIONS.md's own standing
rule): `canvas.ascend_key`, `canvas.descend_key`, `canvas.minimap_ascend` retire while gated;
`canvas.navigate`, `canvas.body_next`, `canvas.body_prev` lose their referent with one body.
Add the click-to-centre verb if Q1 is accepted. Re-render with
`node tools/session/render_actions.js`.

### Scope explicitly excluded

Any change to the Planetary canvas's own draw pass, hit-testing or lens rendering. Resizing the
minimap rect or re-anchoring `selection_band_height`. A second inset. Whether the base view earns
its own lens treatment.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`visual`, a new scripts/verify/minimap_base_render.lua: the inset renders the player's starting
base at max zoom, stays fixed while the primary canvas pans and zooms away from it, and survives the
base being demolished (Q2 fallback). Plus `headless`: with the gate false, no code path reaches
`canvas_level::solar` or `canvas_level::circumplanetary`.

items.title: Persona counsel costs ~1 s per econ tick — profile the blackboard export vs the Lua bench, then bound it
items.summary: Measured 2026-08-12 (Debug, 0 CE world, 35 corps): post_persona_counsel averages ~1,049 ms per econ tick — 93% of the tick — against ~80 ms for convoys + economy + clearing + budget + recorders combined. It was the whole AppHangB1 startup stall (the warm start now suppresses it, app.cpp m_warm_starting), but LIVE PLAY still pays it on every econ tick: a visible hitch at speed, growing with corp count. Cost = per due corp, export_corp_blackboard + every non-verdict pack's Lua evaluate.
items.design: First profile WHICH half dominates: the C++ blackboard export (visibility-honest world scan per corp) or the sol2 pack evaluation (Lua per pack per corp). The step_economy phase accumulators (app.hpp step_economy_phase_ms, added 2026-08-12) give the total; add a lap inside post_persona_counsel to split it. Then bound whichever wins: cadence is already staggered (corp_strategic_eval_due), so candidate levers are (a) evaluate only corps whose counsel channel is OPEN in the chat panel (the player reads one channel at a time; benches for unwatched corps produce lines nobody sees), (b) cap due-corps-per-tick, (c) cache the blackboard between eval boundaries, (d) move evaluation off the tick onto a budgeted per-frame slice like the warm start. Lever (a) is the legible one: counsel is presentation (it never touches the world — session_history.cpp header), so skipping unwatched corps changes no simulation state and no determinism. Measure in Release before sizing the fix (NR-180's standing caveat: Debug amplifies).

items.title: The company's answerability - which laws and polity terms an armed trading house operates under, and what breaking them costs
items.summary: Split out of BL-315 (conflict spine) on Ben's 2026-08-13 ruling. BL-315 owns how force reaches an outcome; this owns what the company is ANSWERABLE TO while using it. The same law classes the militia framing named - embargo, basing rights, conscription - but with the direction of agency inverted: terms the company is subject to and must route around, not instruments it wields.
items.design:
## Why it is its own item

It was BL-315's third strand, and it was blocking a buildable item behind an unbuilt one:
at 0 CE there is no live law system to be subject to. Splitting it lets the conflict spine
be built now, and lets answerability arrive when there is law for it to read.

## What it owns

The terms an armed trading house operates under, and the consequence of breaking them.
The direction of agency is the whole point - an embargo is something procurement must be
routed around, basing rights are granted rather than granted BY, a levy applies TO the
company's recruitment pool.

It is also where BL-315's identity ruling cashes out. Ben, 2026-08-13: the same company
reads as army, mercenary or pirate depending on policy - so the reading is a function of
whose terms it operates under, and which it has broken. That derivation belongs here, not
in the conflict spine.

## Design owed

Which law classes bind a company rather than a nation; what a breach costs (standing?
contract access? interdiction?); and whether the army/mercenary/pirate reading is
per-polity (one nation's privateer is another's pirate) or global. The per-polity reading
is the richer one and is probably right, but it is not settled.
